The mid-term evaluation for Enabel, of November 2024, states that the Enabel project PASS Sutura started the digitalisation with recruited consultancy firms, with the Ministry of Health's digital health directorate involved. PASS Sutura is a Belgian bilateral project with EUR 14.5 million for health over 2022-2026, and a Netherlands co-financing of EUR 3.2 million to 31 March 2025 puts particular emphasis on digitalisation. On 8 July 2026 the health minister opened the workshop validating the costed roadmap of the Schéma Directeur National de la e-Santé 2025-2029.

Tiers in use. By November 2024 the project had set up digitalisation, including computerised medical records and billing, in the integrated health centres (CSI) and district hospitals of Dioundiou, Gothèye and Gaya.

Where data is digitised. Enabel states that a hospital information system built around a computerised medical record was put in place at the district hospitals of Gaya and Gothèye after field missions in February and April 2024.

Last twelve months. At the workshop of 8 July 2026 the Directorate of e-Santé presented OpenClinic, its project for a hospital information system and computerised patient record, as already under way.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The evaluation of November 2024 places the digitalised health centres in the project's three target health districts only. In September 2018 the ministry's strategy reported electronic patient record activity in two health districts, Gaya and Gothèye, of 72.

Not held. No count of health centres using the computerised record is held, and no denominator. Nothing held says whether the record is made at the point of care or keyed afterwards, and no sites or counts are given for OpenClinic.

NGA.short: 100 of Lagos State's 326 primary clinics record care electronically as it happens (May 2025); there is no national figure.
NGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare's Nigeria Digital Health Architecture of December 2025 sets interoperable electronic health record systems across all levels of care as its first pillar. In the memorandum signed with the United States on 19 December 2025, Nigeria commits to roll digital medical records out in 20% of facilities by 2026 and 100% by 2030, and the United States plans approximately US$28 million for an enhanced electronic medical record system over 2026-2030.

Tiers in use. The Minister of State for Health told the National Council on Health on 20 November 2025 that over 200 hospitals are integrated with electronic medical records systems. In Lagos State an EMR was in use in primary health care centres in May 2025.

Where data is digitised. In May 2025 the Lagos State Primary Health Care Board described its EMR as working "at the point of care". The federal architecture of December 2025 states that health data systems remain largely siloed and paper based, especially in public facilities.

Last twelve months. On 16 September 2026 the minister of state for health said the electronic medical record systems deployed in health facilities are fragmented and that minimum standards would be set and enforced.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Lagos State Ministry of Health reported on 22 May 2025 the EMR platform deployed in 100 of the state's 326 primary health care facilities.

Not held. No national share or count of primary clinics using an EMR is held; the figure is Lagos State's alone, and the over 200 hospitals have no denominator or tier. No shared record on a unique identifier is evidenced, and Nigeria's own commitment to data systems is not broken down to the EHR.

RWA.short: All 42 district hospitals used electronic patient records in 2023, and the national system reached most public facilities by 2026; shared records are not shown.
RWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Rwanda Biomedical Centre slides of April 2026 present eBuzima as the national system for all public health facilities, served from the Ministry of Health's own domain. In a memorandum signed on 5 December 2025 and running from April 2026 to December 2030, the government commits to expand national EMR systems across all health facilities. The United States plans to allocate US$6,806,292 over 2026 and 2027 to the e-Buzima rollout, and Rwanda commits to pay the ongoing licensing, cloud and hardware costs the United States does not.

Tiers in use. A survey of April and May 2023 found all 42 district hospitals using an electronic medical record system, 35 of them OpenMRS. King Faisal Hospital Rwanda, a referral hospital in Kigali, runs an Integrated Health Management Information System that gives each patient a single record, the Tony Blair Institute reported in July 2026.

Where data is digitised. The April 2026 slides describe eBuzima as centralised, web-based and synchronising records across public facilities.

Last twelve months. By 8 April 2026 eBuzima had been rolled out to the majority of public health facilities, with its HIV key-population and PrEP modules running in one Kigali pilot site.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Tom Frieden wrote in a piece published in September 2026 that eBuzima is in more than two thirds of health centres. The 2023 survey found 71 of 215 randomly sampled public health centres (33.0%) using an electronic medical record system.

Not held. No unique patient identifier and no record retrieved at another facility is established. No count of facilities using eBuzima is held, nor who enters the record at the health centres or where it is keyed.

SDN.short: A hospital system with electronic medical records was launched at two hospital sites on 11 May 2026; routine use is not yet shown.
SDN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Communications launched the hospital management system (HMS) on 11 May 2026 as their own programme, on the Sudan News Agency's report. ICTworks' directory, as of July 2026, lists the Sudan eHealth Strategy of the WHO Global Observatory's 2014 cycle as the operative digital health instrument and states that no replacement has been promulgated.

Tiers in use. Phase one of the HMS started on 11 May 2026 at two hospital sites, Al-Nao hospital in Khartoum state and the diagnostic centre of Gedaref hospital, ahead of gradual expansion to health institutions in other states.

Where data is digitised. An MSc thesis at Sudan University of Science and Technology, of March 2021, states that hospitals in Sudan had no electronic medical records and kept patients' health records on paper.

Last twelve months. A directive published on 30 March 2026 has the Prime Minister ordering hospital systems digitised within two weeks through a first pilot phase at Soba teaching hospital and Gedaref hospital. The HMS launched on 11 May 2026 includes an electronic patient record and an electronic medical record.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The first phase directed in March 2026 covers two hospitals only, with wider expansion left to a later phased plan. The thesis of March 2021 states that government clinics had no electronic medical record and depended wholly on paper records.

Not held. Whether the two sites are in routine use, the hospitals' level and where the record is entered are not established. No funding source is named for any system, and no sites or counts are held for SudaHealth, the Khartoum State platform.

SEN.short: The patient record runs only at pilot sites, in 1% of the 102 health centres (October 2025); health posts are not counted.
SEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The World Bank, in a paper of January 2026, names the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene as lead agency, deploying the electronic medical record. The ministry's sector policy letter of 25 March 2025 sets the generalisation of the computerised patient record under its Health System Digitalisation Programme 2023-2029. The record is a core activity of the US$46 million health component of the IDA-financed Senegal Digital Economy Acceleration Project.

Tiers in use. The health ministry states that the record, which it calls the Dossier Patient Informatisé, has been in use since November 2024 at the Thierno Birahim Ndao regional hospital in Kaffrine. We Are Tech Africa reported on 30 April 2025 a completed pilot at two hospitals, the Khadim Rassoul health centre and the HLM Fass health post.

Where data is digitised. At the Kaffrine hospital the patient is created in the system at registration and the doctor enters observations directly into it after the consultation, on the ministry's account, since November 2024.

Last twelve months. The World Bank records that a pilot of the record across 51 health centres had not started as of December 2025, delayed by disagreement between the health and digital ministries.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The World Bank's results framework gives 1 per cent of the 102 district-level health centres as using electronic medical records at 31 October 2025. An electronic record was available for 200,000 primary care patients at the same date.

Not held. Retrieval of a patient's record at another facility is not stated, and the 1 per cent counts health centres only, with health posts outside it. Nothing held says whether the 51-centre pilot began in 2026.

SLE.short: Electronic records run at one government hospital and one clinic (2026); a national system is not known to have been bought.
SLE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. OpenMRS's case study of April 2026 describes the PIH EMR as Partners In Health's own OpenMRS distribution. The National Health Compact of 6 December 2025 commits the Government to roll out Electronic Medical Records to all medical facilities by 2030 and names a Ministry of Health directorate as lead. The Ministry's request for expressions of interest of 18 December 2025 states that a donor grant finances the initial phase.

Tiers in use. The case study states that Koidu Government Hospital, a referral centre, uses the PIH EMR and that the EMR has run at Wellbody Clinic since 2015. The Ministry reported on 11 October 2023 that it and Smart Systems Sierra Leone Ltd had launched an EMR pilot at Connaught Hospital in Freetown.

Where data is digitised. The case study states that the EMR at the Maternal Center of Excellence in Koidu is entered at the point of care, with retrospective entry also possible.

Last twelve months. The Maternal Center of Excellence opened on 14 February 2026 with the EMR covering all its inpatient wards. On 18 December 2025 the Ministry's project unit asked firms to express interest in deploying an OpenMRS-based EMR across 300 health facilities.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The case study of April 2026 names one clinic using the PIH EMR, Wellbody Clinic. The Compact of 6 December 2025 gives a baseline of 5 health facilities implementing the system, in a network it puts at about 1,463 public facilities.

Not held. What share of primary clinics keep patient records electronically is not held, nor the present state of the pilots at other primary facilities. The Compact's baseline of 5 facilities is undated, and the Ministry's national EMR is not shown procured.

SOM.short: Two electronic record systems run in over 40 facilities (April 2026) and 111 primary facilities (2025); their share of all clinics is unknown.
SOM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. By its own account the Ministry of Health developed RAAD as a national electronic health record for primary healthcare, implemented between 2023 and 2025. Its bulletin for July to September 2023 says the pilot was supported by the Government of Sweden through SPIDER. The Caafimaad+ Digitalized Data System (C+ DDS) is run by the CaafimaadPlus consortium of ten NGOs, in partnership with the Federal Ministry of Health, and funded by EU Humanitarian Aid, as the consortium stated in April 2026.

Tiers in use. The ministry's case study places RAAD in public primary healthcare facilities only, between 2023 and 2025.

Where data is digitised. RAAD captures clinical data as routine care documentation, in place of an average of 15 paper forms, on the ministry's case study of 2023 to 2025. The consortium said in April 2026 that C+ DDS replaces manual reports with real-time entry and makes a family's record available at any facility on the system.

Last twelve months. The consortium reports growth from a five-facility pilot in mid-2024 to over 40 facilities by April 2026.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. In April 2026 the consortium reported C+ DDS operational in over 40 facilities across 9 regions and more than 25 districts of South-Central Somalia. The ministry's case study reports RAAD deployed in 111 public primary healthcare facilities across six states between 2023 and 2025.

Not held. No count of all primary clinics is held to set either figure against, and the two systems' facilities are not shown to be separate. No plan naming an electronic medical record, no unique patient identifier and no tier for the C+ DDS facilities is held.

SSD.short: Only an HIV treatment register at five sites is held; nothing shows general patient records, electronic or paper, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not held. No electronic medical record in use is held, and no dated statement that patient records are on paper at every tier. The 22.4% of health facilities that the February 2025 assessment records with facility-wide electronic systems comes with no system named.

STP.short: A patient record was piloted at the central hospital and in one health area in 2022; whether it was extended is not known.
STP.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Health Development Plan 2023-2032, dated September 2022, sets a strategic axis on expanding what it calls the single clinical process to the whole national health system. The Joint SDG Fund programme's final report of 26 July 2022 states that the Single Process module for patient files was developed inside DHIS2, the Ministry of Health's main information software, and that rolling it out beyond the pilot will be done with funding from other donors.

Tiers in use. In September 2022 the plan placed the record in a pilot phase at the Ayres de Menezes central hospital and the Água Grande Health Area.

Where data is digitised. The report of July 2022 states that patient data is entered from reception through the nurses and doctors, each patient's file reached by a bar code sticker and scanner.

Last twelve months. The plan of September 2022 states that the pilot is to be evaluated before expansion to the whole national health system.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. At 26 July 2022 the Single Process had not been rolled out to other districts and still needed consolidating in the first pilot district, Água Grande. The plan states that computerised clinical records are to be introduced gradually through a pilot model of health centres and the central hospital.

Not held. Nothing is dated after September 2022: whether the pilot was evaluated, consolidated or extended beyond Água Grande is not established. The health area's facilities are not named and no count of facilities using the record is given.

SWZ.short: A shared electronic record runs in 73% of all health facilities (2026); it stays at stage 3 because no current plan or budget was found.
SWZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Data.FI described the Client Management Information System (CMIS) in April 2026 as an open-source, government-owned electronic medical record. The Ministry of Health's HMIS unit describes itself as custodian of the digital health systems, with its own in-country developers working on CMIS. Data.FI, a PEPFAR-funded USAID agreement, reported for the period ending March 2024 that it funds and carries out CMIS system development, security assessment and facility network support.

Tiers in use. Data.FI described CMIS in April 2026 as in use in the outpatient department of Piggs Peak Government Hospital and at local health clinics.

Where data is digitised. Data.FI said in April 2026 that clinicians open a client's full record on a unique ID number at their point of service, and that the record is available to clinicians at another clinic if the patient moves district.

Last twelve months. The HMIS unit reported in June 2026 that the integration of CMIS with eLMIS runs for ART medicines only and is ready for a facility-level pilot. In the first quarter of 2026 its developers completed training that produced automated, FHIR-aligned data flows from CMIS to DHIS2.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Data.FI said in April 2026 that CMIS is used in 73% of the country's health facilities, with 233 live sites. For the period ending March 2024 it reported CMIS in use at 75% (247 of 327) of healthcare facilities.

Not held. No current plan naming CMIS and no domestic budget line for it is held. The 73% is a share of all health facilities with no denominator given, and no count of primary clinics alone is held.

SYC.short: A ministry system that includes electronic medical records has run since the end of 2021 (reported January 2024); who uses it is not known.
SYC.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Seychelles Nation reports the health minister saying on 17 October 2023 that the Ministry of Health is investing in an Electronic Health Information System encompassing Electronic Medical Records, the ministry's name for it. The National Health Strategic Plan 2022-2026 sets specific objective 6.8, "Implement eHIS", and names the Health Care Agency as lead entity, with the Ministry of Health and the Public Health Authority contributing.

Tiers in use. The minister said in October 2023 that the system is to be accessible to all health professionals throughout the health system.

Where data is digitised. At its digital health visioning meeting of 22 January 2024 the ministry said it was trying to link the system with laboratories and X-ray so that doctors get results on their computers.

Last twelve months. A ministry press release carried by Seychelles Nation in January 2024 states that the system has been operational since the end of 2021.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The 2022-2026 plan sets three go-live phases, the first being client registration and appointments across all relevant units.

Not held. The tiers using the system, where the record is entered and the primary clinics using it are not established. Finance is not stated, and nothing dated inside the last twelve months is held.

TCD.short: The ministry signed a partnership for electronic medical records in its hospitals (reported August 2026); no facility is yet shown using one.
TCD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Public Health and Prevention leads the electronic medical record initiative, with HISP Rwanda as technical assistant, HISP Rwanda states. Guinéenews reports that Kouma Academy supplies its Visa Medical record under a model in which the company invests its own funds in the equipment and infrastructure of public hospitals, and has an agreement with the ministry.

Tiers in use. The partnership Guinéenews reported on 13 August 2026 is for the national digitalisation of the country's hospitals with the Visa Medical digital medical record.

Where data is digitised. HISP Rwanda describes the record whose implementation it supports as a patient-centred Dossier Médical Électronique.

Last twelve months. On 15 April 2026 the ministry's Secretary-General chaired a high-level meeting devoted to modernising the patient medical record, and by 13 August 2026 Kouma Academy had signed its partnership with the ministry.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Guinéenews describes the partnership as covering the country's hospitals.

Not held. No electronic medical record is held in use at any facility: no tier, no place of digitisation and no clinic figure. Neither the partnership nor the ministry's initiative carries a deployment, a pilot site, a budget or a timetable.

TGO.short: The World Bank reported in December 2025 that no electronic health record system was in place.
TGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The World Bank's additional-financing paper of 24 December 2025 states that since October 2025 the health ministry has been responsible for the health and insurance systems layer, including the electronic health record (EHR). The financing pays EUR 866,112.50 on establishment of the system and EUR 173,223 for every 10 contracted facilities with an EHR.

Tiers in use. The paper records "No" at December 2025 for the establishment of an electronic health record system.

Where data is digitised. The Togo Digital 2025 strategy of April 2021 plans a digital and centralised medical record, as something to be developed.

Last twelve months. On 24 December 2025 the World Bank put forward additional financing, a EUR 60.6 million credit and US$11 million in grants, with new conditions for establishing an EHR in facilities contracted under the national health insurance scheme, starting with a pilot.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The paper's results framework gives a baseline of 0 facilities contracted with the national health insurance scheme holding an EHR at December 2025, out of about 335 contracted facilities.

Not held. No source states in terms that patient records are on paper at every tier, and the baseline does not cover facilities outside the insurance scheme. Where records are digitised is not held.

TUN.short: Electronic records are fully used in 50% of university hospitals and 32% of regional hospitals (2025), with pilot sites in one region's primary care.
TUN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. WHO Tunisia stated in April 2024 that the Ministry of Health's Information Technology Centre develops and implements the hospital information management system, with a focus on electronic medical records. The draft National Health Policy of 2019 calls for the generalisation of a single, digitised medical record. The first-line record, which the programme calls the DMI, was developed under Essaha Aziza, a Ministry of Health and European Union programme.

Tiers in use. The World Bank's project document of 2 April 2025 gives the record as fully installed and used in 50 per cent of university hospitals and partially used in the other 50 per cent, and as fully operational in 32 per cent of regional hospitals, partially used in 52 per cent and absent from 16 per cent. In district hospitals it is neither installed nor used.

Where data is digitised. Of primary health care, the same document states that the health system remains largely paper-based and that the DMI pilot faces connectivity and functionality issues.

Last twelve months. The Ministry of Health confirmed on 21 July 2026 that the Sahetna.tn portal, through which citizens are to reach their medical records, had completed technical validation and a cybersecurity audit; it was not yet in service.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Essaha Aziza states that it monitored the DMI's deployment on pilot sites in Nabeul. DH Arab, on the ministry's account at 25 September 2026, has 99 healthcare facilities at various stages of implementing electronic medical records.

Not held. No count of hospitals or of primary clinics using the record is held; the 99 facilities carry no tier and the Nabeul pilot sites no number. The plan is an uncosted draft of 2019, and no domestic budget line for the record is named.

TZA.short: A government system runs in 23.25% of all health facilities (2023 survey); records are not shown to be shared between facilities.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The mid-term review of the Health Sector Strategic Plan V, published in March 2025, states that the Ministry of Health developed and launched Afya eHMS for all regional hospitals and plans to phase out the vendor-dependent Medipro and E-Medical used in zonal and specialised hospitals. It records that the Digital Health Strategy 2019-2024 had run out and its 2025-2030 successor was still being developed.

Tiers in use. The Citizen reported on 1 September 2026 that electronic medical record coverage had reached 100 percent of national, specialised, zonal and regional referral hospitals, and that adoption had expanded across district hospitals, health centres and dispensaries. The mid-term review of March 2025 states that all 28 regional hospitals use Afya eHMS.

Where data is digitised. The ministry's guidelines of May 2019 state that most confidential health data is held in health facilities in paper-based registers.

Last twelve months. The Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Health said on 1 October 2025 that the country has an integrated electronic medical records system linking a patient's information from community level through health centres and district hospitals to national level.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The mid-term review, citing the SARA survey of 2023, gives 23.25% of all health facilities using GOT-HoMIS, the government's facility system, against 44.9% of health centres and 10.63% of dispensaries. In March 2025 it states that more than 3,000 primary health care facilities use it as their electronic medical record system.

Not held. Nothing held establishes where the patient record is digitised or whether it can be retrieved at another facility. No financing is stated, no dated event falls in the last twelve months, and no community system is shown exchanging with the EMR.

UGA.short: The ministry's electronic record ran in referral and general hospitals and seven health centres in 2025; records are not shown to be shared.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Health's guidelines of 18 September 2024 name the ministry as owner of the Electronic Medical Records System. The US-Uganda memorandum signed on 10 December 2025 names eAfya and ClinicMaster as the Government of Uganda's electronic medical records and sets a functional EMR in all facilities down to Health Centre III by 2028. Under it the United States plans US$113,102,289 for data systems over 2026-2030.

Tiers in use. The ministry says that as of 2025 the EMR is in referral and general hospitals and in some health centres. In Kiryandongo district it was in use in September 2026 at the general hospital, Nyakadoti Health Centre III and Mpumwe and Apodorwa Health Centre IIs.

Where data is digitised. The in-charge of Nyakadoti Health Centre III said on 19 September 2026 that patient data must be captured in the EMR at every stage of the visit. A census of all 265 government Health Centre IVs and hospitals, published in October 2025, found 94.3% keeping both paper and digital patient records.

Last twelve months. On 31 March 2026 Makerere University's METS programme handed the UgandaEMR repositories to the Ministry of Health. Health workers told a baraza on 19 September 2026 that the EMR was slowing care in Kiryandongo facilities because of poor connectivity, unstable power and too few computers.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The ministry counts 5 Health Centre IVs and 2 Health Centre IIIs using the EMR as of 2025.

Not held. Nothing held shows a record retrievable at another facility, or what share of primary clinics use the EMR; hospital coverage is disputed between the ministry and a census of government facilities. No domestic budget line for the EMR is held.

ZAF.short: Hospital systems run in five provinces and 308 Western Cape primary facilities use electronic records (August 2025); there is no national count.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Minister of Health told Parliament on 1 August 2025 that the National Department of Health is developing a single common Electronic Medical Record for primary health care facilities. The department's bid document of March 2026 says it developed the EMR itself and that its Digital Health Unit directs implementation.

Tiers in use. The same reply counts Clinicom in 53 Western Cape hospitals, the eHealth system in 42 KwaZulu-Natal public hospitals and HMS2 in 16 Free State hospitals. It states that Mpumalanga, North West, Limpopo and Northern Cape are not implementing such systems at hospitals.

Where data is digitised. The department describes its EMR, in March 2026, as capturing clinical information at the point of care, verified against the patient's identifier in the Health Patient Registration System.

Last twelve months. In March 2026 the department invited bids to scale up its EMR to all fixed primary health care facilities in eight provinces within 18 months. The Free State Department of Health won the Public Sector Digital Innovator Award for deploying its primary health care EMR, SAnews reported in May 2026.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Minister's reply states that the National EMR beta ran in 36 primary health care facilities between 22 October 2024 and 13 February 2025 and that Western Cape's Primary Health Care Information System is implemented in 308. It counts 3,333 primary health care facilities reporting to the 2024/25 Ideal Clinic Assessment.

Not held. No count of primary facilities using the national EMR in 2026 is held, and no total of hospitals against which the provincial counts can be set. Nothing held shows a record retrieved at another facility, and no funding source is named.

ZMB.short: An electronic record system was in use at 877 of 3,540 health facilities of all kinds (April 2025); the share of primary clinics is unknown.
ZMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Global Fund's case study of April 2025 states that the Ministry of Health developed SmartCare and describes it as co-financed by the Global Fund. SMART Zambia's national coordinator said on 7 July 2026 that government aims at full national coverage of SmartCare Pro.

Tiers in use. SmartCare 2.0 Hospital Edition went live as a pilot at Ndola Teaching Hospital on 27 April 2026. Interviews of May and June 2019 found some larger health centres and hospitals collecting data in the electronic health record, in select districts.

Where data is digitised. The programme managers' presentation of March 2025 describes SmartCare Pro as capturing the patient encounter at facility level, on a central server that identifies each client uniquely and tracks patients between facilities. The implementers described in January 2026 a nurse at a rural clinic in Kafulafuta identifying a patient by fingerprint to reach his record.

Last twelve months. ITWeb Africa reported on 16 July 2026 that SmartCare Pro and SmartCare 2.0 will be migrated to the government-owned GovLink network, with three Copperbelt hospitals connected first.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Global Fund states that SmartCare Pro is in use at 877 health facilities, against 3,540 health facilities in Zambia, at April 2025. The March 2025 presentation puts SmartCare Legacy and SmartCare Plus together in approximately 1,800 healthcare facilities. SMART Zambia's national coordinator said on 7 July 2026 that SmartCare Pro has been deployed in approximately 80% of health facilities nationwide.

Not held. No count or share of primary clinics using SmartCare is held: every figure counts health facilities of all kinds, and the 80% is of deployment, with no numerator or denominator. Use at the primary tier rests on 2019 interviews and one rural clinic, and nothing held shows a record retrieved at a second facility in practice.

ZWE.short: An electronic record system ran in 1,254 health facilities of all types in August 2025, out of 1,900 planned; shared records are not shown.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Global Fund said in August 2025 that the Government of Zimbabwe has been developing a national EMR system since February 2015, culminating in Impilo, for use in public health facilities. The ministry's National Health Strategy 2021-2025 commits to supporting the deployment of what it calls the electronic health record (Impilo) system. The Global Fund has put over US$43.1 million into digital health in Zimbabwe since 2014, US$9.85 million of it in the 2024-2026 grant cycle.

Tiers in use. The Permanent Secretary for Health and Child Care told The Sunday Mail on 17 November 2024 that the facilities with Impilo are spread across provinces and districts and include clinics, hospitals and other health centres.

Where data is digitised. A 2025 abstract on the DHIS2 community site states that Impilo captures real-time clinical and administrative data for services including HIV testing, antiretroviral therapy and maternal and child health, stored in centralised repositories and a national data warehouse.

Last twelve months. The Herald on 23 September 2026 described Impilo as the Ministry of Health's own electronic health records platform.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Global Fund reports 1,254 health facilities implementing Impilo as of August 2025, with deployment planned for all 1,900 health facilities. The Permanent Secretary put deployment at 1,178 health facilities on 17 November 2024. The Matabeleland South provincial health team reported 110 of the province's 153 health facilities (71.9%) with Impilo fully functional in May 2025.

Not held. Nothing held says an Impilo record can be retrieved at another facility. The counts are of facilities of every type where Impilo is deployed, not of primary clinics entering records, and no strategy current at 30 September 2026 is held.

AGO.short: Since 2023 births are entered digitally at offices in Luanda and three other cities; most offices use paper, and the digital count is not known.
AGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Justice and Human Rights runs civil registration through its directorate DNIRN and introduced RCI, as it names its civil registration system, in 2023. Presidential Decree 267/24 of 28 November 2024 approved a plan to December 2026 for a single database fed daily by civil registration. Nascer com Registo, the government's maternity registration programme, is financed by the European Union, ANGOP reported on 4 March 2026.

Events registered digitally. Births have been registered in RCI since 2023 at civil registration posts. Angola told the registrars general on 18 July 2026 that biographic and biometric data are collected when the birth entry is issued.

How the record is made. In RCI the birth is entered at the post, in a system with a centralised database. The older SIRC has no central database and the majority of civil registration units still rely on paper records, as of 2024.

Last twelve months. Novo Jornal reported on 5 May 2026 that identification and civil registration posts in almost the whole country had been without their system for four months. A civil registration post opened on 3 March 2026 in the provincial hospital's maternity at Mbanza Kongo.

Local offices doing the digital entry. RCI is in Luanda's registries and in one post each in Huambo, Benguela and Lubango, as of 2024. The World Bank's diagnostic counts 39 civil registration units in Luanda province and at least 255 in the country in 2023.

Not held. No source counts the offices registering in the central system, and deaths in a digital system are not described. No source says the outage reported on 5 May 2026 has ended.

BDI.short: Digital civil registration runs in about twelve pilot communes in 2026, most acts still on paper; how the pilot record is made is not known.
BDI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The interior ministry presents the civil registration reform and its pilot digitalisation as the government's, with the World Bank, UNICEF, UNECA and UNDP as supporting partners, in its presentation of 18 July 2026. Its director general for territorial administration put the platform's cost at about BIF 15 billion on 6 May 2026.

Events registered digitally. The project launched at Rumonge on 19 July 2024 is for the digital registration of births and deaths at the commune's civil status service, at its seat and in its zones.

How the record is made. The ministry's director general told the African registrars general on 18 July 2026 that the majority of civil-status acts are still recorded in physical registers and that Burundi has no single national database of them. The ministry's director general said on 6 May 2026 that the legal framework still rests on manual registration procedures.

Last twelve months. On 6 May 2026 the ministry presented a digital platform for civil registration and biometric identity card production, its infrastructure nearly complete and awaiting a decree. On 11 August 2026 it stated that the government continues to scale up the platform.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The ministry's presentation of 18 July 2026 records a pilot digitalisation project in 12 communes. On 10 August 2026 thirteen communes had a biometric registration system, with civil registration digitalised in pilot communes.

Not held. No source says the system is past its pilot, how the digital record is made in the pilot communes or where it is held. No plan with a current period and no domestic budget line for the platform is on record.

BEN.short: Births are registered digitally at maternity desks in ten pilot health facilities since August 2025; how other local offices make the record is not known.
BEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. ANIP, the national identification agency, runs the one-stop birth registration desk with its own teams and the Ministry of Health's health workers. Benin's playbook of May 2026 states that ANIP is attached to the Presidency and is in charge of the population register and the national civil-status file. ANIP began the reform with the support of the WURI project and UNICEF.

Events registered digitally. From 20 August 2025 the declaration and registration of a birth are done on site in about ten public health facilities. In six months 17,071 children were declared there and 13,069 registered, ANIP reported on 24 February 2026.

How the record is made. Desk agents at Natitingou and Djougou register the child in the system at the maternity, working on tablets and centralised databases, La Nation reported on 16 July 2026. Paper declaration forms remained in use during the pilot.

Last twelve months. The pilot ended in February 2026 and a consolidation phase is running in the same ten facilities, with generalisation three to four months behind the initial calendar, ANIP's director general said on 16 July 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The desk's pilot was launched on 20 August 2025 at CHU-MEL Cotonou and runs in ten public health facilities. On 24 February 2026 the desk was running in 10 health facilities, with gradual national scale-up among the prospects.

Not held. How ANIP's communal units and the civil-status centres make the record is not described, so deaths and offices beyond the ten pilot facilities are not established. No plan with a period is on record.

BFA.short: Birth-entry software was deployed in 170 civil registration centres in 2025; the total number of centres, and how many register in it, is not known.
BFA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Direction générale de la modernisation de l'état civil trains commune agents on the platform it calls VENEEM. The Stratégie nationale de l'état civil 2023-2027 was adopted by joint order on 25 January 2024. In 2024, 2.52% of its financing came from the state budget, 33.46% from local authorities and 64.01% from partners.

Events registered digitally. The country's delegate told an Abidjan symposium in December 2024 that births are declared directly from health centres through a national application. Agents of the commune of Pouni were trained from 31 August to 2 September 2026 to enter births, marriages and deaths.

How the record is made. The Pouni training covered entering events in real time by smartphone, at central offices and secondary centres alike. A November 2024 account says the platform captures events where they occur, on computers and smartphones. The Code des personnes et de la famille, in its 2025 text, institutes a national digital civil-status register.

Last twelve months. Agents of the commune of Koloko were trained on the software and given equipment, as reported on 22 June 2026. On 25 June 2026 the director general for the modernisation of civil status said deployment in communes was continuing.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The ministry reported the software deployed in 30 main and 140 secondary centres in 2025, and in 20 main and 96 secondary centres in 2024.

Not held. The total number of centres, how many of the 170 register in the software and whether the 2025 count includes 2024's. Where the record is held, and whether deaths are entered beyond one commune's training.

BWA.short: A national system registered births and deaths in 2024; how many of the 35 district offices enter records in it is not known.
BWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Department of Civil and National Registration of the Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs operates the registration offices and holds the records of the Births and Deaths Registration System. Its recurrent provision of P108,505,050 for 2026/27 covers the system's maintenance among others. A 2019 health ministry roadmap scheduled a registration strategic plan for 2021-2026.

Events registered digitally. The system registers births, stillbirths and deaths, and was the source for the 49,180 births and 14,070 deaths registered in 2024.

How the record is made. Statistics Botswana in August 2026 calls the system "partially automated and decentralized", designed to give real-time statistics and integrated with the National Identification System, which has assigned a birth registration number at birth since 2003. A September 2015 report says births and deaths records pass online from local and regional offices to a central repository.

Last twelve months. The minister told Parliament on 6 March 2026 that of about 15 hospital kiosks set up to register births on site, 9 were operating and 6 had closed, chiefly for lack of staff. On 24 February 2026 he said online registration of births and deaths was built and would go live with the 1-Gov platform.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The department operates 35 district registration offices and 17 on-site registration points at hospitals and clinics, as Statistics Botswana reported in August 2026. Electronic on-site registration had opened in 13 hospitals by September 2015.

Not held. How many of the 35 district offices and 17 on-site points enter records in the system, and whether the entry is made at the office. No plan in force is held, and the kiosk closures are undated.

CAF.short: A civil registration application was still being developed in July 2026 and offices register on paper; the number of pilot offices is not known.
CAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The territorial administration ministry, through its Direction Générale de la Décentralisation et de l'État Civil, is preparing the deployment of a civil registration application with CIVIPOL as technical operator. The Politique Nationale de l'État Civil was adopted by the Head of State on 4 April 2025. The supporting MODERO project is financed by the European Union.

Events registered digitally. The software under development is to cover births, marriages and deaths, the director general said on 18 July 2026. UNICEF's profile of 2017 gives births and deaths as processed by hand on paper.

How the record is made. The director general described an all-paper system on 18 July 2026, with 70% of civil registration centres without electricity. Civil registration registers were distributed to communes of the Ouham, and registers for declaring births to the maternity of Bossangoa university hospital, UNDP reported in April 2026.

Last twelve months. In July 2026 the ministry was preparing to deploy the application, which was not yet deployed. An operational map of 45 centres had been validated by 18 July 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The country's delegate told an Abidjan symposium in December 2024 that the digitalisation of civil status was at the pilot phase and should extend to 40 localities in 2025.

Not held. No office is shown entering a birth or a death digitally. How many offices were in the pilot, what it piloted and the period the national policy covers are not held.

CIV.short: In March 2026 the registrar said 98 per cent of civil status centres were computerised and connected; whether any registers births digitally is not known.
CIV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. ONECI, the national civil status and identification office, is the executing arm of the national civil status policy, the Minister of the Interior and Security said on 16 June 2025. A convention of 2 March 2026 implements the Stratégie nationale de l'état civil et de l'identification. The 2026 finance law appropriates FCFA 500 million from domestic revenue for modernising civil status.

Events registered digitally. The software ONECI supplied to the centres, which AIP names Citiweb, is intended for the digital registration of births, marriages, deaths and other civil status acts.

How the record is made. The World Bank said on 18 September 2025 that the registry is still on paper. The decree of 2 October 2019 keeps the paper register as the legal record and permits acts to be established by computer beside it.

Last twelve months. At the end of 2025 ONECI supplied all town hall and sub-prefecture centres with computers carrying the software, and began training agents. From 27 to 29 July 2026 it trained 44 agents of the Gôh region.

Local offices doing the digital entry. ONECI's director general said on 2 March 2026 that 98 per cent of civil status centres were computerised and connected to the software, and on 11 August 2026 that its Système national de gestion de l'état civil was deployed in 699 centres.

Not held. The evidence does not say that any centre registers a birth in the software: every figure is of centres equipped, computerised or with the system deployed, and neither the 98 per cent nor the 699 comes with a total of centres. How the record is made at an equipped centre is not established.

CMR.short: In September 2026, 60 of 432 principal civil status centres were digitised, 13.9 per cent; the share of all local offices is not known.
CMR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. BUNEC, the national civil status office, works under the supervision of the decentralisation ministry. Its National Strategic Plan for the Modernisation of the Civil Status System 2025-2029 was launched on 11 September 2025. The equipment in the communes comes through UNDP projects, Legal Identity II in the East Region and a Denmark-funded one in ten municipalities.

Events registered digitally. UNDP reported in September 2025 that Maroua 3 council issues birth, marriage and death certificates, producing birth certificates on the system while the parent waits. In the East Region birth acts were being produced in the system UNDP names SIGEC by August 2026.

How the record is made. Each East Region commune receives its own server, workstations and network with the software installed, UNDP reported in August 2026. In an interview published on 8 October 2026 BUNEC's Director General describes paper as the dominant process, with digital registration in selected councils only.

Last twelve months. On 7 January 2026 Limbe I Council issued the first birth certificate from a digitalised system in the North-West and South-West regions. By August 2026 two East Region centres, Bertoua 1er and the Bertoua City Council, were in production.

Local offices doing the digital entry. On the figures BUNEC's Director General gave on 14 September 2026, 60 of the country's 432 principal civil status centres were digitised, 13.9 per cent, against 42 in April 2022. The country also has 2,439 secondary centres.

Not held. The share of all local offices is not published: the 60 are counted against principal centres only, and the secondary centres are outside the figure. The evidence does not establish that a record made in a commune is held in the national register, and it states no national budget line.

COD.short: In August 2025 one commune of the capital was piloting digital civil registration; whether any birth or death has been registered digitally is not known.
COD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Interior and Security is responsible for civil registration through its Civil Registration Division, as of March 2019. The one pilot is executed by four United Nations entities and financed by the UN's Joint SDG Fund, UNFPA reported on 18 August 2025. A national civil-registration strategy and a master plan for digitising the centres were still to be written on 1 October 2026.

Events registered digitally. UNFPA stated on 18 August 2025 that the Masina pilot aims to automate the collection and management of data on births, marriages and deaths.

How the record is made. Government terms of reference posted on 3 April 2026 state that the civil registers are mostly manual and are not integrated into any central file. In March 2019 the Civil Registration Division reported that each act is written on paper with four carbon copies.

Last twelve months. A UNDP tender closing on 25 April 2026 sought a consultant to assess the digitalisation of civil registration and support the design of digital registration tools. On 23 July 2026 a sector office in Walikale, North Kivu, had been out of birth registers for several months.

Local offices doing the digital entry. One commune, Masina in Kinshasa, has a pilot at its municipal civil-status office, UNFPA reported on 18 August 2025. In March 2019 the Civil Registration Division counted 979 local offices, 102 urban and 877 rural, none using a computer or mobile device.

Not held. No fact says an event has been registered digitally: the Masina pilot's births and deaths are stated as its aim, and its own dates and results are not given. No count of offices is held newer than the 979 of March 2019.

COG.short: A civil registration system was built and validated by September 2026 but no office uses it; whether older urban systems still run is not known.
COG.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The state agency ACSI designed and built the civil registration system Congo calls SIFEC for the Interior ministry's territorial administration directorate. On 20 February 2026 the validation workshop's main recommendation was that the human, material and financial means to deploy it be provided. The World Bank's Congo Digital Acceleration Project counts an operational civil registration database among its results.

Events registered digitally. None. SIFEC's Births, Marriages and Deaths modules were under validation in February 2026, and the World Bank scored a national digital database of civil registration records not operational at 31 May 2025.

How the record is made. On paper: in February 2026 the Interior ministry's security adviser called the system long manual and fragmented. In 2021 the World Bank found electronic records stored locally in civil registration centres of Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, and rural areas largely paper-based.

Last twelve months. On 20 February 2026 a workshop at Kintélé validated 17 recommendations on SIFEC. On 7 August 2026 the Interior minister told the Senate its rollout was imminent. On 22 September 2026 ACSI handed the system's operating documents to the territorial administration directorate.

Local offices doing the digital entry. None. After the handover of 22 September 2026 seven steps remained, user training and deployment among them. In 2020 the World Bank counted 2 of Brazzaville's 10 civil status offices as digitised.

Not held. Whether the electronic records kept in some Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire centres in 2020 and 2021 are still kept. Who pays for SIFEC's deployment, and the period of the civil status digitisation roadmap.

COM.short: In 2026 offices register on paper while a digital system is studied and costed; when its three-centre pilot starts is not known.
COM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of the Interior carries the modernisation project Comoros calls AMECC, with the French embassy and UNICEF. By 14 August 2026 the country held a costed modernisation plan and a national mapping of civil registration centres. France and UNICEF financed the work to that date, and national institutions validated a residual financing need of EUR 9,009,900.

Events registered digitally. None. Births, marriages and deaths are registered in paper registers, and the digital system, an eCRVS, is only proposed, by a preliminary study validated on 25 March 2026.

How the record is made. In August 2026 the system was still largely dependent on old paper registers. In January 2026 the Minister of the Interior said acts are made on secured printed forms produced abroad, with recurring shortages.

Last twelve months. The study preceding digitalisation was launched in Moroni on 2 October 2025 and validated there on 25 March 2026. On 11 March 2026 the Council of Ministers did not adopt the draft decree for a national civil status agency. A UNICEF-recruited consultant ran a resource-mobilisation mission from 30 July to 16 August 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. None. The preliminary study covered 37 civil status centres and proposes a pilot in three, at Moroni, Mutsamudu and Fomboni. Of the 37, fewer than half have stable electricity and one in five has internet access.

Not held. When the three-centre pilot starts, and the period the costed plan and the 2024 strategic plan cover. Whether any office keeps records other than on paper.

CPV.short: In 2017 offices in all 22 municipalities entered births and deaths digitally, in urban centres only; whether records reach the national register is not known.
CPV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. UNICEF's profile, compiled to November 2017, names the Directorate of Registries, Notaries and Identification of the Ministry of Justice as the authority registering births and deaths. Decreto-Lei 43/2007 places the civil registry database in that directorate's ownership.

Events registered digitally. Births and deaths. UNICEF's profile, compiled to November 2017, states that all vital events are recorded directly in the computer. NOSi's catalogue of 2025 lists a Civilian ID System that collects and processes civil registry data on births, marriages, deaths and stillbirths.

How the record is made. In 2017 events were recorded in applications located in the civil registry conservatórias, with a certificate issued immediately. The Civil Registry Code of 2014 requires entries in electronic form, held in a national civil registry database, and allows paper only when the system is unavailable.

Last twelve months. NOSi's catalogue of 2025 describes the Civilian ID System as a stream linking the civil registries to other government systems.

Local offices doing the digital entry. UNICEF's profile, compiled to November 2017, puts the applications in the conservatórias of all 22 municipalities, 22 of 22. Registration stations exist only in the urban centres of those municipalities; mobile teams reached rural communities during the birth registration project.

Not held. Whether the entry made at the conservatória is held in the national register in practice. Any share of offices, or rural share, newer than 2017; any fact on ownership, plan or finance from the last three years, and any event in the last twelve months.

DJI.short: Nine civil-status sites in Djibouti-Ville have entered births and deaths digitally since 2011, as stated in 2024; digital entry outside the capital is not known.
DJI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ville de Djibouti states that it has held the civil-status service since the Ministry of the Interior transferred the competence in 2008, and that its communes have exercised it since 2011 through SIGEC, as the city names its computerised civil-status system. Terms of reference of February 2024 place a diagnostic of SIGEC and a budgeted action plan under PROGOUV, a EUR 8 million governance support project for the city.

Events registered digitally. The city stated on 28 April 2024 that the registration of births, marriages, divorces and deaths in Djibouti-Ville has rested since 2011 on software for entering, transmitting and using civil-status data. The February 2024 terms of reference state that maternity antennas enter birth declarations in the system and the central centre draws up death and marriage acts.

How the record is made. By the city's account of 2024, civil-status agents have fed its database continuously since 2011 as they make new entries. The terms of reference place the data on a central server in a room of the Hôtel de Ville.

Last twelve months. The city reported on 28 April 2024 a diagnostic of SIGEC by an international expert, commissioned under PROGOUV.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The February 2024 terms of reference list nine civil-status sites, all in Djibouti-Ville: the Mairie's central centre, three commune centres and five antennas in maternities.

Not held. Nothing dated 2025 or 2026 says any office outside Djibouti-Ville enters digitally, and no national count of offices, no plan and no event of the last twelve months is held. A 2025 ESCWA survey, held only in summary, says local offices hold no electronic records of births or deaths, which disagrees with the city's 2024 account.

DZA.short: Births are registered in a national digital register across 1,541 communes, a 2019 count; the share of local offices entering digitally is not known.
DZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Law 14-08 of 9 August 2014 creates the national automated civil-status register under the Ministry of the Interior and Local Authorities. A university article published on 10 October 2025 places the register within the e-municipality programme of the national e-Algeria strategy, which it dates 2008 to 2028. The ministry's presentation of July 2026 lists the availability of financing among the levers of the digitalisation.

Events registered digitally. The same presentation states that since 2018 each newborn has a birth act and a national identification number at the end of its registration, the number generated automatically from the register. The ministry's deck of 19 June 2019 shows the register holding three databases, of births, deaths and marriages.

How the record is made. The 2019 deck places entry, control and update at commune level, with 48 wilaya databases for error correction and a national database at the ministry. Under the 2014 law each commune still inscribes acts on three paper registers kept in duplicate and transmits a digitised copy of every act to the national register.

Last twelve months. In July 2026 the ministry presented the register as its own, created in 2014, with unified national governance of civil-status data.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The 2019 deck shows 1,541 commune databases where entry, control and update are done. The 2025 article states that paper documentation persists alongside the digital services.

Not held. The 1,541 is a 2019 count of commune databases with no total of local offices, communes and their annexes together, and nothing held says the entry is made at the commune office when the event is registered. No event of the last twelve months and no rural figure is held.

EGY.short: Births and deaths are entered digitally at 4,571 health offices, as stated in 2026; the share of all offices is not known.
EGY.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The development plan for fiscal year 2026/27, as Youm7 reported it on 2 August 2026, credits the Ministry of Health and Population and the bodies concerned with developing the electronic birth and death registration system and names it within the digital-transformation axis of the national family development project. Law 143 of 1994 gives the Civil Status Organization of the Ministry of Interior the registration of births and deaths.

Events registered digitally. Egypt's presentation to the 2026 APAI-CRVS registrars-general meeting states that a central database for births and deaths runs on a secure platform and directly updates the statistics office's population clock.

How the record is made. A conference paper on the system implemented in 2017 states that data entry is done at the health office, which prints the birth or death certificate once entry is complete, with the offices linked online to a central database. The 2026 presentation describes automated health offices feeding the central database.

Last twelve months. An article of 20 January 2026 reports that the health ministry instructed all health affairs directorates to unify and improve the quality of data entered on the automated births and deaths registration system at health offices.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The 2026 presentation gives full nationwide automation of 4,571 health offices across the 27 governorates. The planning ministry's report of 2 August 2025 says 4,666 health offices are electronically linked.

Not held. No total of health offices is held against the 4,571 or the 4,666, and no rural share is published. Egypt's undated answers to a WHO questionnaire published in 2025 describe paper at registration points and electronic entry at the governorate centre, which disagrees with the 2026 account.

ERI.short: Births and deaths were handwritten at local offices and entered in regional electronic registers one level up in 2017; current practice is not known.
ERI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Eritrea has developed a five-year Strategic Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Plan for 2024-2028, recorded by the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child in observations adopted in April 2026.

Events registered digitally. Births and deaths are both registered in the sub-zoba's digital database after entry in the kebabi's handwritten register, according to a Dutch foreign ministry report of February 2017 cited by the Danish National ID Centre, which adds that death registration has no fixed or automatic routine.

How the record is made. A birth is first entered in the handwritten family register at the local kebabi office, which issues a transfer letter that the parents take to the sub-zoba office, where the data is entered into the database and the hard copies are archived (2017). A death goes the same way, by a "death letter" from the kebabi to the sub-zoba.

Last twelve months. The death certificate issued by the local municipality is computerised and carries a registration number, the US State Department said in 2025.

Local offices doing the digital entry. Each of the six zobas keeps an electronic population register, first introduced in zoba Maekel in 2003 and updated by the 54 sub-zoba administrations, while each of about 2,000 kebabi administrations keeps a handwritten family register, the Danish National ID Centre states, citing the European Asylum Support Office in May 2015.

Not held. How a birth is entered today, how many offices do the digital entry, who owns and pays for the registers, and whether the 2024-2028 plan names a digital system. The record-making facts date from 2015 and 2017, and nothing is held for the last twelve months.

ETH.short: Digital registration of births and deaths is in pilot, in Addis Ababa and 1,300 of 19,202 kebeles in 2025; use beyond pilots is not known.
ETH.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Immigration and Citizenship Service is the registration organ, with structures from federal to the lowest administrative level, under Proclamation No. 1370/2025 of 18 March 2025. The national eCRVS, which Ethiopia calls the Civil & Family Registration System, is homegrown, driven by the Prime Minister's Office and carries a three-phase rollout plan (July 2026).

Events registered digitally. The national eCRVS lists birth and death registration and certificates among its services, alongside marriage, divorce and adoption (July 2026).

How the record is made. The eCRVS is a decentralised, multi-tenant system on a shared architecture in which city administrations and regions provide all services, with offline access, rural connectivity, power and tablets listed as gaps (July 2026). Civil registration is mainly paper-based and manual, three copies of the form passing from kebele to woreda to the Service (July 2025).

Last twelve months. On 5 December 2025 the mayor of Addis Ababa launched the Integrated Civil Registration and Residency Service Technology and announced full implementation in 50 woredas from 8 December.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The eCRVS rollout begins with a pilot in Addis Ababa, then Amharic-speaking regions, then the rest of the country (July 2026). A tablet system, ME-CRVS, has been piloted in 1,300 kebeles and health facilities, in a country the Service counts at 19,202 kebeles, 70% of which provide civil registration (July 2025). In Addis Ababa the city agency's digitisation was in a pilot phase in 21 of 116 woredas in January 2025.

Not held. Whether any digital system is past its pilot outside Addis Ababa, which rollout phase the eCRVS had reached by July 2026, and whether the entry is made at the office. No source of finance is stated for the eCRVS, and nothing establishes that registering a birth feeds the Fayda number.

GAB.short: No office registered births or deaths digitally in May 2026; a system is being prepared with funding to 2028; its first offices are not known.
GAB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Law 008/2022 of 15 June 2022 makes the Centre National de l'Etat Civil (CNEC) the public service that builds the digital, biometric and centralised civil register and directs the civil status centres. The World Bank's Digital Gabon Project keeps US$10.5 million for digitalising civil registration, in a project closing on 30 June 2028 (June 2026).

Events registered digitally. No digital registration of births or deaths is in service: the Gabon Digital general coordinator said in September 2026 that the digital platforms for managing civil registration come second, after the decisions on the rules for attributing identity.

How the record is made. Civil registration runs on manual procedures, which the coordinator said the reform should break with (September 2026). The World Bank described the civil registry as entirely paper-based in June 2021.

Last twelve months. The project's technical assistance was recruited in April 2026 and a mapping exercise to prioritise the departments whose offices will register digitally was under way at 31 May 2026. On 28 September 2026 an inter-ministerial workshop opened at Ntoum to define the conditions for putting the CNEC into operation.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The World Bank reports no administrative department with a civil registration office digitally registering vital acts at 31 May 2026, against a target of nine departments by June 2028.

Not held. No pilot office is named, and the count held is of departments, with no total, not of offices. No domestic budget line is stated, and the CNEC is not yet in operation.

GHA.short: Births were registered digitally at two Accra registry centres in 2024; how many offices do so, and how the record is made, is not known.
GHA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Births and Deaths Registry, under the Ministry of Local Government, develops and administers the births and deaths registration system under Act 1027 of 2020. A Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Strategic Plan for 2025 to 2030 was validated at a workshop in July 2025. The 2025 budget gives births and deaths registration GHS 7,409,170, of which GHS 6,909,170 is internally generated funds and nothing is from donors.

Events registered digitally. Births in Ablekuma West, a municipal district of Greater Accra, are registered on the Registry's digital registration platform, 1,722 of them from March to October 2024. The Registry's electronic database is the source of its count of 50,992 deaths registered in 2022.

How the record is made. In 2022 a district registration officer entered a death in the register and completed a paper form, which was scanned into an electronic database at the national office.

Last twelve months. In a 2026 report the Eastern Regional Registrar said officers are expected to complete birth registrations digitally in communities and that poor internet connectivity is a major obstacle.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The two registry centres of Ablekuma West, Dansoman and Gbegbeyise, registered 1,045 and 677 births on the digital platform from March to October 2024. In April 2025 the Acting Registrar said the Registry was taking steps to digitise all offices.

Not held. No national count or share of local offices entering births digitally is held, and no source states how a birth record is made or whether it is entered at the office. No dated event falls in the last twelve months.

GIN.short: Commune offices made digital birth certificates in September 2026, when a paper shortage halted printing; how many offices do so is not known.
GIN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The 2023 civil status law makes the ministry in charge of civil status responsible for buying, installing and maintaining the equipment of civil status centres. In September 2026 an unnamed company in charge of the secure paper was reinstalling the data centre. An evaluation for Enabel found in April 2026 that national technicians had no access to the source code of the register system it names E-RENEC, and that the project closed in February 2026 with no maintenance or operating budget secured.

Events registered digitally. Ratoma commune's civil status officer said on 2 September 2026 that commune offices establish digital birth certificates on secure paper.

How the record is made. The officer said the system depends on a data centre, whose relocation disturbed it while registrations continued. In March 2026 Conakry's 13 communes received paper registers for the year's registrations, and in February 2026 registrars still used paper in parallel.

Last twelve months. By 2 September 2026 printing of digital birth certificates had been halted for about two weeks by a stockout of secure paper.

Local offices doing the digital entry. Ratoma's officer said the secure paper serves to establish digital birth certificates in all the communes of Guinea. Enabel, in a text published in August 2023, described a digital national civil registry piloted in ten communes.

Not held. No count or share of offices is held, and no source states that the entry is made at the office or whether the digital birth certificate is the registration of the birth or a secure copy of it. No plan is stated.

GMB.short: Births are registered on a central digital system, with 79 local offices holding digital registers in 2025; the total number of offices is not known.
GMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Health holds the mandate for birth registration, under the Registrar General of Births and Deaths. The system was deployed under a World Bank lending operation that ended in August 2025. A National Digital ID and Digital Transformation Strategy for 2023 to 2028 went to a validation workshop in May 2024.

Events registered digitally. The Registrar General said that by June 2026 over 1.4 million people were registered in the system he calls the eCRVS and issued a birth certificate. A 2025 World Bank diagnostic has its birth module in operation and a marriage module developed.

How the record is made. The diagnostic describes a centralised register, with registration carried out locally by Ministry of Health staff in each district and civil registration offices holding digitalised registers. Before 2022 the processes were manual and paper-based.

Last twelve months. A Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Bill had its first reading in the National Assembly on 5 March 2026. Registrations on the system rose from 1.17 million in February 2023 to over 1.4 million in June 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The diagnostic counts 79 civil registration offices with digitalised registers issuing birth certificates in 2025, beside 258 health facility outlets where Ministry of Health staff carry out registration.

Not held. The total number of civil registration offices is not held, so the 79 have no share, and no source states that the record is keyed at the registration point when the birth is registered. No death module is in operation and no domestic budget line is stated.

GNB.short: One Bissau office registers births and deaths digitally in 2026, and health posts in three regions register births; the share of offices is not known.
GNB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The system the country calls SIREC was implemented at the Ministry of Justice's Direção-Geral de Identificação Civil, Registo e Notariado, launched in January 2025. The digital transformation strategy approved in March 2025 names the civil registry among the services to consolidate and expand. UNDP reports for 2025 that the Swiss Confederation, the European Union and Portuguese Cooperation financed it.

Events registered digitally. Officials at the Santa Luzia Civil Registry Office in Bissau record births, marriages and deaths directly on SIREC, UNDP said in April 2026. Health workers at registration posts in hospitals and health centres register births on a tablet, UNICEF reported in September 2025.

How the record is made. Santa Luzia has replaced paper register books with workstations connected to the national platform, with records entered directly and held centrally, on UNDP's account of April 2026.

Last twelve months. In the first quarter of 2026 Santa Luzia became the first civil registry office in the country to operate entirely digitally. In June 2026 a mobile caravan was to take birth registration on SIREC to 16 communities in Cacheu, Oio, Bafatá and Gabu.

Local offices doing the digital entry. UNDP names one office, Santa Luzia, as entirely digital in April 2026. UNICEF said in September 2025 that digital registration is available in hospitals and health centres of Bissau, Tombali and Quinara. The statistics office counts 13 conservatórias and 80 registry posts in its yearbook for 2018 to 2022.

Not held. The number of offices and posts entering records digitally, against the country's total, is not held. Nor is the platform used at the health-service posts, or whether it is connected to the national register.

GNQ.short: A digital pilot registers births in Malabo only, since 2018, and the seven regional offices use paper in 2024; its present state is not known.
GNQ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Justice put the system it calls SIREC into service in December 2018, with the support of UNICEF and the European Union. The statistics strategy for 2022 to 2026 sets a civil registry system established as an expected result. The World Bank said in 2024 that funding to extend the digital registry to the mainland is lacking.

Events registered digitally. The pilot in Malabo allows the digital registration of new births, on a platform developed to collect births and deaths, the World Bank said in 2024.

How the record is made. The seven regional offices collect and store data by manual, paper-based processes, and local judges registering at commune level share manually collected data with them, on the same account of 2024.

Last twelve months. The World Bank's diagnostic, published in 2024, reports UNICEF as saying the pilot is operational and functions well.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The pilot was launched in late 2018 exclusively in the capital, Malabo, by the Ministry of Justice with UNICEF.

Not held. Nothing on the pilot is dated after 2024. How the pilot makes the record, and how many offices in Malabo use it, are not held.

KEN.short: More than 270,000 births were registered digitally from hospitals in two months of 2026; how many offices or hospitals use the system is not known.
KEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Civil Registration Services sits in the Ministry of Interior and National Administration's State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services, under an executive order of January 2023. ESTDEV, the implementing partner, said in September 2026 that it funded the development of the digital birth registration service, with project activities funded by Germany and the European Union. A costed plan for 2018 to 2022 listed the upgrade and rollout of the registration system among its high priorities.

Events registered digitally. More than 270,000 births were registered in two months through the new digital birth registration solution, ESTDEV said in September 2026. The principal secretary said the same system may in future be used for deaths.

How the record is made. Parents confirm the birth and enter the data while still in the hospital, and it goes directly to the population registry, with the certificate issued the same day or within days, on ESTDEV's account of September 2026.

Last twelve months. The solution's first two months were the first time Kenyan parents could register a birth online, ESTDEV said in September 2026. The Star reported in March 2026 that the Civil Registration Service led the validation of the Births and Deaths Registration Bill 2025, which gives a legal framework for digital registration.

Local offices doing the digital entry. Civil Registration Services reported for 2023 that it had offices in 153 of 380 sub-counties, where registration was manual, on paper registers.

Not held. The number of hospitals or offices using the system is not held. Nor is whether the entry is made at a registration office, or a plan for the present period.

LBR.short: County teams registered births online in 2024, with deaths added to the platform; how many of the 58 centres enter them is not known.
LBR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Health registers and certifies births and deaths through its Bureau of Vital Statistics, by its report for 2024, and that year developed a National Birth and Death Registration Policy. UNICEF, the World Bank and other partners helped it decentralise birth registration, and the Ministry says budget constraint limits its ability to sustain the birth registration centres.

Events registered digitally. The Ministry's report for 2024 says birth and death registration have been integrated into the DHIS2 platform. As of 2023, 93,031 birth registrations had been recorded in DHIS2, which the Ministry gives as 67 per cent of all birth registrations and certifications. UNICEF Liberia calls the system the Birth Registration Information Management System.

How the record is made. County birth registration teams register and certify births online on a web-based platform, the Ministry reports for 2024, collecting application forms from health facilities and returning certificates to them. In May 2024 the World Bank found most services at the 15 County Service Centers, birth registration for ages 0 to 12 among them, remained paper-based.

Last twelve months. In 2024 the Ministry trained over 45 birth registration staff on the platform and procured 35 antivirus licences for county birth registration computers.
