Local offices doing the digital entry. The Ministry says birth registration centres have been established in all 15 counties since 2010. UNICEF Liberia in December 2024 counted birth registration services in all 15 counties and 58 centres.

Not held. How many of the 58 centres enter births on the platform is not known, and no source gives a total of local offices. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months, and whether the 2024 policy names the platform is not stated.

LBY.short: All civil registration offices were automated and linked to one database, the health ministry said in 2022; whether events are entered there is not known.
LBY.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Civil Registration Authority, of the Ministry of Interior, manages the collection of births and deaths data and issues the legal documents, by the health ministry's vital statistics report published in 2022. In January 2025 the Ministry of Interior said the Authority was continuing the Intilaqa project, under the supervision of the Attorney General's office, matching the electronic data in the civil status system against its paper originals.

Events registered digitally. The Authority's electronic system recorded 231,670 births and 31,051 deaths in 2020, says the Ministry of Health's Health Information Centre, which generated its report for that year from it.

How the record is made. The Health Information Centre's report, published in 2022, states that all of the Authority's offices are fully automated and electronically linked to its centre, working through a single automated system on the same database.

Last twelve months. On 1 March 2026 the Attorney General's office reported that he had discussed with the head of the Authority the latest completed phase of the project to create the electronic civil registry database.

Local offices doing the digital entry. All of the Authority's offices are automated and linked to the single database, the Health Information Centre said in 2022; its report counts 12 branches, 133 issuing offices and at least 380 service offices.

Not held. Whether a birth or death is entered at the office when it is registered is not stated, and the office figure is undated and gives no rural share. No plan or finance for the system is held.

LSO.short: Births were registered digitally at 30 health-facility stations in three districts in 2026; the total number of local offices is not known.
LSO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Department of National Identity and Civil Registry, in the Ministry of Home Affairs, is the lead agency for civil registration, it said in July 2026. Its presentation lists a costed CRVS Strategic Plan 2026-2030 as still to be developed during 2026. The Government's 30 birth registration stations had support from the Government of Japan and UNICEF, UNICEF Lesotho said in August 2026.

Events registered digitally. Birth registration stations in health facilities are supported by an SMS-based platform for registering births, UNICEF Lesotho said in August 2026. The Ntlafatsa Bana project's digital birth registration system registers births on tablets, UNICEF reported in June 2025.

How the record is made. UNICEF reported in June 2025 that real-time tablet-based registration, operated by village health workers and civil registration officers, has replaced manual processes. A World Bank note of May 2022 says all 15 enrolment centres that allow for birth registration are linked to a central server.

Last twelve months. UNICEF Lesotho reported on 5 August 2026 that 30 birth registration stations had been established in health facilities in Maseru, Berea and Leribe. In July 2026 the Department listed nationwide scale-up of digital birth registration as an action for 2026-2027.

Local offices doing the digital entry. UNICEF Lesotho counts 30 birth registration stations in health facilities across three districts, in August 2026. The World Bank note of May 2022 counts 15 enrolment centres, across Maseru and each of the 10 districts.

Not held. No total of local registration offices is published, so neither count is a share, and the two counts are of different systems. Where the SMS platform's record is held, and whether deaths are entered at any local office, is not known.

MAR.short: Offices enter births and deaths in a ministry system said in 2024 to reach every office; the share of offices registering digitally is not known.
MAR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of the Interior runs the civil-status management system, which it calls SGEC, under its civil-status modernisation programme, reported in October 2024. The World Bank's Municipal Performance Program, which counts a civil registry back-office system among its results, is financed by an IBRD loan with AFD co-financing and closes on 31 December 2026.

Events registered digitally. The ministry said in October 2024 that SGEC handles birth and death declarations digitally, and that over 1,300,000 acts had been declared or issued from it.

How the record is made. By the ministry's October 2024 account, an entry agent at the civil-status office enters acts in SGEC and the civil-status officer checks and validates them. In October 2025 Hespress reported communes short of the paper registers essential for registering births.

Last twelve months. The World Bank gives the civil registry back-office system as operational in 59 of 97 participating municipalities on 30 June 2024 and unchanged on 30 January 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The ministry said in October 2024 that SGEC was generalised to all the Kingdom's civil-status offices. In October 2025 its circular called for staff to be trained on the national digital platform, access to which was to be opened shortly.

Not held. No count of offices registering digitally against the country's total of offices is held. The modernisation programme's period and budget, and whether an identifier is assigned at birth in practice, are not held.

MDG.short: Communes register births digitally, 336 of them in December 2025; the share of all communes this represents is not known.
MDG.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A decree of 2 December 2020 set up the Centre National d'État Civil et de l'Identité under the technical supervision of the Interior ministry to keep the national digital civil status and identity registers. The digital registration system was rolled out under the PRODIGY project, financed by an IDA credit of US$133 million and a GFF grant of US$3 million and closing on 30 June 2026.

Events registered digitally. By December 2025 61,892 birth certificates carrying a unique identity number had been issued through the digital civil registration system, which Madagascar calls SIECM.

How the record is made. Communes themselves use SIECM to register civil-status events and issue birth certificates with a national unique number, the World Bank reported in December 2025; the system's offline module had been in demonstration since November 2025.

Last twelve months. Communes using SIECM rose from 75 to 336 in the six months to December 2025. In March 2026 the Unité de Gouvernance Digitale described the birth registration platform as being deployed progressively at national scale.

Local offices doing the digital entry. In December 2025 336 communes were using SIECM, which the World Bank gives as 40% of the project's target; a further 112 communes had been trained and were not yet operational.

Not held. The share of all communes using the system is not held, nor where the record is kept. No digital death registration is reported, and nothing held says what has funded the system since the project's financing closed on 30 June 2026.

MLI.short: Births were registered on paper in July 2026 and a digital platform had ten pilot areas named; whether any has started is not known.
MLI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. An ordinance of 14 February 2025 creates the Agence nationale de Sécurisation des Actes d'Etat civil, a national public establishment, to develop and maintain the systems that manage civil status acts, with an initial endowment from the State. UNICEF says it has supported the Government's efforts to digitise birth registration since 2022.

Events registered digitally. A platform approved by December 2024 is to consolidate births, deaths and marriages, which UNICEF's representative describes as the first fully digital platform for civil status events.

How the record is made. In July 2026 the head of digitalisation at the National Directorate of Civil Status described the birth chain as paper: community health workers fill village notebooks, the declaration agent sends a slip to the civil status centre, and the officer there draws up the act.

Last twelve months. In July 2026 the directorate named complete digitalisation of the system as a priority.

Local offices doing the digital entry. By December 2024 the National Directorate of Civil Status had identified ten pilot areas for the platform, taking in civil registration centres, health facilities and courts.

Not held. No office is shown entering an event digitally, and whether the pilots have started is not held. No current plan and no budget line for the system is held.

MOZ.short: Births are entered directly at district offices and all 68 conservatories were digitised by 2025; the share of local offices entering digitally is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Directorate of Registries and Notaries holds the main database of the system it calls e-RCEV. A ten-year plan, SIRCEV 2019-2029, targets 80 per cent birth registration of children under five, the National Director said in 2025. Cooperation partners support 100 new posts in maternities, mainly with computer equipment, reported in September 2026.

Events registered digitally. The registrar's portal, read in August 2026, gives the registration of births and deaths as the system's initial focus. UNICEF's evaluators state that births and deaths were registered electronically as of October 2018. The National Director listed registering deaths in the community as a current challenge in 2025.

How the record is made. District registration offices connect to the central platform and enter registrations directly into the central database, UNICEF's evaluators stated in 2021. At 534 community registration points births and deaths are taken on forms that the district office then processes.

Last twelve months. Jornal Notícias reported on 24 September 2026 that the justice sector is installing 100 civil registration posts in health units with maternity wards, beside about 250 birth registration posts already working, about 25 per cent of some 1,000 health units.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The National Director of Registries and Notaries said in 2025 that all 68 civil registration conservatories are digitised. By 2018 the system was functional in 75 districts and 183 administrative posts, UNICEF's evaluators state.

Not held. No share or count of local offices making the digital entry, set against a total, is held: the 68 conservatories are counted as digitised and the posts below them are left out. Whether the new maternity posts enter the record digitally is not held.

MRT.short: By law births are recorded centrally at citizen reception centres, 153 of 168 equipped in 2021; whether centres enter births digitally is not known.
MRT.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The interior ministry's DGCT stated in November 2022 that civil status acts are the exclusive competence of ANRPTS, the population register agency. The Prime Minister inaugurated the agency's integrated system for the population register and secure documents on 3 August 2021; the agency's director general put its cost at 12,157,616 euros.

Events registered digitally. Law 2025-011 of 24 February 2025 requires a birth to be declared within 60 clear days at the Centre d'Accueil des Citoyens and has civil status acts signed electronically. Law 2011-003 has births and deaths declared at the centre and recorded in the central database.

How the record is made. Article 18 of Law 2011-003 provides that declarations of civil status events are recorded immediately in the database of the central system. Under the law of 24 February 2025, heads of centres receive declarations only at the centres, where they are registered.

Last twelve months. The Civil Status Code was amended on 24 February 2025, treating the recorded data as data of the Registre National Biométrique des Populations.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The ANRPTS director general said on 3 August 2021 that 153 citizen reception centres had been received and equipped out of 168 to be built in communes and administrative centres, to receive civil status declarations, enrol people and hand over secure documents.

Not held. Nothing outside the law is held saying that a centre enters a birth digitally when it is declared, and the count of centres is of those equipped in August 2021. Nothing is held on ownership, plan or finance since November 2022, or on the last twelve months.

MUS.short: Births and deaths are registered online at computerised civil status offices, 35 listed in 2019; the share of all offices is not known.
MUS.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The CSD System is the Civil Status Division's own, under the Prime Minister's Office and headed by the Registrar of Civil Status. The Division spent Rs 387,863,137 against government budget estimates of Rs 445,600,000 in 2023/2024, with no donor named. Its Strategic Directions 2023/2024 name the revamping of the CSD System.

Events registered digitally. The Division's report for 2023/2024 states that the CSD System, operational since November 2001, provides for the registration of births, deaths and marriages. Offices opened on 6 and 7 September 2025 for the registration of births and deaths during the system's revamp.

How the record is made. The Registrar stated in June 2019 that civil events have been registered online since November 2001 at computerised civil status offices, a national identity number being generated on each birth registered. The record is stored in the Division's single Civil Status Database, the Division stated in 2024.

Last twelve months. The Civil Status Division announced on 2 September 2025 that its CSD System was being revamped, with a transition period in which delays might be met.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Registrar listed 35 Civil Status Offices by district, two of them in Rodrigues, in June 2019, and described them as computerised.

Not held. No share of offices making the digital entry is held: the 35 computerised offices of 2019 are a count with no total, and the communique of September 2025 gives no count. No current plan naming the system and nothing dated inside the last twelve months is held.

MWI.short: Births and deaths were entered digitally at 87 local service points in five districts in 2025; the share of local offices is not known.
MWI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Registration Bureau, under the Ministry of Homeland Security, is the body responsible for civil registration, by its plan of September 2025. That plan, for 2025 to 2030, costs civil registration at MWK 66.06 billion and names limited domestic budget allocations as a threat to the service. UNDP's basket fund spent USD 2,107,228 on digital identity and civil registration in 2025.

Events registered digitally. In 2025 registration officers at Traditional Authority offices began registering community births and deaths on a mobile application the Bureau calls Nzika. Kits at district registration offices register births and deaths and print certificates, by the plan of September 2025.

How the record is made. The district kits synchronise with the central system over the government network or mobile links, by the same plan. Nzika runs on mobile kits with biometric authentication, works offline and is integrated with the national civil registration system, UNDP reported for 2025. In some remote areas the digital birth system had not fully replaced paper by 2024, and forms were lost or not entered centrally.

Last twelve months. Nzika registration moved from pilot to 87 service points during 2025, and national rollout is planned for 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. UNDP counts 87 service points in five districts in 2025, against 277 Traditional Authorities and 138 Sub-Traditional Authorities in 28 districts listed for expansion by 2030. Certificate printers were in 58 health facilities in 2025.

Not held. No share of local offices registering digitally is published, and the health facilities registering births carry no total. The gap in remote areas has no figure.

NAM.short: Local offices enter births and deaths in the national register, as reported in 2024; the share of offices doing so is not known.
NAM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security registers births and deaths on the National Population Registration System, the statistics agency said in April 2024. The system was developed in the country with its own resources, by a UNICEF and UN case study of September 2023. Cabinet approved a civil registration plan for 2015/16 to 2020/21 in 2015.

Events registered digitally. The system's death module was deployed in 2012 and its birth module in 2013. The statistics agency counts 85,853 births and 24,388 deaths registered and captured on it in 2021.

How the record is made. The local civil registration office captures the application on the system and issues the certificate, and the record is available in real time across the 14 regions, the agency said in April 2024. Of births registered in 2021, 68.9 per cent were captured within 14 days, and 89.6 per cent of deaths.

Last twelve months. In December 2025 the ministry said it had deployed its staff to 24 state hospitals to issue birth certificates right after delivery.

Local offices doing the digital entry. Some registration offices in remote areas lack computers or internet connectivity, which delays capture, the statistics agency said in April 2024. Birth and death registration took place at local registration centres and 24 health facilities and hospitals, by the case study of September 2023.

Not held. No count or share of local offices registering digitally is published, and the gap at remote offices has no figure. No civil registration plan later than 2020/21 is named.

NER.short: The digital register ran in 101 of 266 communes in December 2024, a share of communes; digital death registration outside Niamey is not known.
NER.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The civil-status system belongs to the Interior Ministry's Direction Générale de l'état civil, des Migrations et des Réfugiés, the ministry said on 11 August 2026. A civil registration strategic plan covers 2023 to 2027. The computerisation announced that day sits under the WURI-Niger project, which the World Bank finances.

Events registered digitally. The ministry's database for the five arrondissements of Niamey holds 72,459 births and 6,524 deaths registered in 2023, by the statistics office.

How the record is made. Events are declared at the centres and passed to the commune, where agents key the acts on machines connected to a server at the ministry's directorate, and each validated act is saved there, the statistics office wrote of 2023. Acts are printed on secured paper from the computerised system, by the government's communiqué of 22 April 2026.

Last twelve months. An ordinance of 22 April 2026 provides for the national civil-status register, and its decree followed on 18 May 2026. On 11 August 2026 the ministry announced the computerisation of all communes and declaration centres and a new platform as works to come.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The computerised system was in production in 101 of 266 communes and communal arrondissements in December 2024, by the statistics office, and the government counted 102 communes on 22 April 2026. Only towns in urban areas had electronic civil registration databases in 2023.

Not held. Digital registration of deaths is not established outside Niamey. Whether the declaration centres in villages and health facilities are computerised is not stated, and the gap between urban and rural offices has no figure.

NGA.short: Births and deaths are entered digitally at ward and local government offices from July 2026; the share of local offices doing so is not known.
NGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Population Commission runs the registration and its centres, and said in July 2026 that the platform is operated under a public-private partnership with a technical partner. The Registrar General's Department lists a Digital CRVS Roadmap for 2024 to 2026. A 2026 programme to speed up birth registration in Kano State is funded by the Government of the Netherlands.

Events registered digitally. Births and deaths have been registered digitally across the country since 1 July 2026, on the platform the Commission calls VitalReg.

How the record is made. The Registrar General's Department described in July 2026 an officer in ward and local government offices registering the birth on the platform, with real-time reporting of registration data. A registrar in Lagos said in August 2026 that his team takes details on a form when the network fails and calls parents back.

Last twelve months. The Commission says the platform became operational in all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory on 1 July 2026, replacing paper registration.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Registrar General's Department reported 3,372 wards activated and 304 registration workstations deployed at 18 July 2026. The Commission said that month that it has 4,011 registration centres across the 774 local government areas.

Not held. The share of local offices entering on the platform: the wards activated have no total, and the count of registration centres does not say how many of them enter on it. No domestic budget line is held.

RWA.short: Births and deaths are entered digitally at all categories of registration office in 2025, the statistics office says; the rural share is not known.
RWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Identification Agency, under the Ministry of ICT, supervises and coordinates the civil registration system nationally, on the statistics institute's account for 2025. The statistics strategy for 2024/25 to 2028/29 names strengthening the system a top priority. The finance law of 30 June 2026 appropriates RWF 116,184,997 to civil registration for 2026/27, domestically financed.

Events registered digitally. The system the country calls NCI-CRVS registered 356,838 births and 39,355 deaths that occurred in 2025, among the nine events registered through it.

How the record is made. The statistics institute states that in 2025 the system captures events in real time at the site where official registration takes place, as a single point of entry. The Agency states that all civil registers have been available only in electronic format since 17 February 2023.

Last twelve months. Birth registration completeness rose from 90.3% in 2024 to 92.9% in 2025, and death registration completeness from 46.1% to 50.5%. The share of deaths registered within the legal 30 days fell from 96.3% to 89.9% over the same year.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The statistics institute states that in 2025 the system is fully operational at all five categories of registration office: health facilities, cells, sectors, districts and embassies. The Agency counted 3,220 civil registration service points in its procedures of December 2023.

Not held. The statement that the system runs at every category of registration office comes with no count of the offices using it, and no figure gives the rural share.

SDN.short: Births are registered in a national electronic registry, with one local office named in 2026; how many offices enter records, and where, is not known.
SDN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Landinfo's report of March 2023 places responsibility for civil registration with the General Directorate for Civil Registration under the Ministry of Interior.

Events registered digitally. The civil registry centre of South Gezira locality issued an electronic birth certificate at its Al-Hosh office on 17 May 2026. A child's birth is registered in the centralised electronic registry introduced in 2011, on Landinfo's report of March 2023.

How the record is made. Landinfo's report of March 2023 describes a centralised electronic registry in which registration is possible at any civil registry office in the country, a birth being registered there on application against a paper notice of birth.

Last twelve months. The Al-Hosh office resumed work in May 2026 after a stoppage caused by insecurity and displacement, and the governor of Gezira State inaugurated civil registry work in Umm al-Qura locality on 29 April 2026. A lawyer told the BBC in a report of August 2026 that the conflict in Darfur has shut down civil registry offices, and an article of June 2026 states that Khartoum's civil registry has ceased almost entirely.

Local offices doing the digital entry. One office is named as issuing an electronic birth certificate in 2026: the Al-Hosh office, which serves South Gezira locality and its surrounding rural villages.

Not held. Nothing since the war began says how or where the birth record is made, and no total of offices is held beside the one named. Digital registration of deaths is not evidenced, and no governance fact dates from the last three years.

SEN.short: In 2026 civil-status centres register births in one national system, with 77% of 629 centres digitised; the share entering data is not known.
SEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Agence nationale de l'état civil (ANEC), an agency attached to the ministry of Urbanisme, Collectivités territoriales et Aménagement des territoires, deploys the software under a Plan national de remédiation begun in May 2026. The European Union financed the NEKKAL programme, which held its final steering committee on 29 June 2026, and ANEC's budget for 2026 had not been notified by 17 August 2026.

Events registered digitally. On ANEC's data the system held 14,839,577 births and 487,259 deaths at 17 July 2026. ANEC's director general said on 16 September 2026 that health services can register births in it directly from maternities.

How the record is made. ANEC's data describe 437 centres as connected to one system, which it calls the Logiciel de gestion de l'état civil (LGEC), with 5,610 new acts registered in it on 17 July 2026.

Last twelve months. ANEC's director general said in an interview published on 5 August 2026 that the LGEC had passed its pilot phase. By 16 September 2026 deployment was effective in the Dakar, Thiès, Louga, Diourbel, Fatick and Kaolack regions, with Tambacounda and the southern regions to follow in 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. ANEC's director general said on 16 September 2026 that the modernisation process stood at 77% of the country's 629 civil-status centres. ANEC's data at 17 July 2026 put the LGEC in 437 of the 629 centres, 70%, from 98% in the Thiès region to 42% in Kédougou.

Not held. No share or count of centres entering events in the system is held: every figure is of centres digitised, deployed or covered. Whether deaths are entered at the office at registration is not held, and no rural share is given.

SLE.short: In 2023 births were entered digitally at the registration authority's hospital centres and sent to a central registry; the number of offices is not known.
SLE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Civil Registration Authority (NCRA), the state agency formed under the 2016 Act, presented the integrated eCRVS and ID management system as its own in May 2024. Its Director General said in August 2023 that the system was developed with European Union support through UNOPS.

Events registered digitally. NCRA told the ID4Africa meeting of 22 May 2025 that over 80% of its integrated civil registration and identity services are digitised, birth and death registration among the services listed. UNICEF's representative said in August 2023 that its support covered the piloting and scale-up of a mobile application for the notification and registration of births.

How the record is made. UNICEF reported in March 2023 that at NCRA's registration centres in hospitals the child's details are entered with the application when the mother registers the birth, then transferred through the central server, which generates the identification number, to the Central Registry System.

Last twelve months. NCRA's presentation of 22 May 2025 says the 2016 Act mandates the Authority to deliver the integrated civil registration and identity services.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Calabash reported in September 2024 that an NCRA project had distributed 48 laptops and internet modems to 48 selected health facilities across the 16 districts. UNICEF reported in March 2023 more than 200 babies registered a month with the application at Ola During Hospital in Freetown.

Not held. No count or share of offices entering events digitally is held, and death registration with the application is not described. No plan covering the present, no domestic budget line and nothing dated inside the last twelve months is held.

SOM.short: By January 2026 local administrations in 30 districts registered births digitally into one central database; the total of districts or offices is not known.
SOM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Law No. 46, published on 5 April 2026, charges a Directorate under the Ministry of Interior, Federal Affairs and Reconciliation with creating and running a digital registration system with a central database. A government roadmap, reported on 11 August 2025, plans to scale the service to every district, subject to funding and infrastructure, and UNICEF, with the government and Germany, supported the foundational work.

Events registered digitally. The ministry said on 10 August 2025 that the platform enables local administrations to register births, deaths, marriages and divorces digitally. OpenCRVS's country page, published in January 2026, counts 28,391 completed birth registrations.

How the record is made. The ministry announced on 10 August 2025 that local administrations in Jubbaland, Southwest, Hirshabelle, Galmudug and Northeastern State register events on the platform and all records are stored in a centralised national database. OpenCRVS's page, published in January 2026, says the system captures births at the point of occurrence in the districts and linked hospitals.

Last twelve months. The platform, which the ministry calls the Unified Digital Civil Registration Service, was launched as a pilot in 19 districts on 10 August 2025.

Local offices doing the digital entry. OpenCRVS's country page, published in January 2026, states that the system operates in 30 districts and is linked to 160 hospitals.

Not held. No total of districts or offices is held, so no share can be read, and only births are counted as registered. The roadmap carries no period, no domestic budget line is stated, and nothing dated falls inside the last twelve months.

SSD.short: A digital civil registration system was announced in July 2026 and no birth is registered digitally; its design and start date are not known.
SSD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The World Bank's diagnostic of May 2026 gives the Directorate of Civil Registry, Nationality, Passports and Immigration as operator and owner of the planned civil registration system. Its director-general said on 28 July 2026 that implementation would start with support from partners, and named none.

Events registered digitally. The World Bank's May 2026 diagnostic found that birth registration is yet to be implemented and birth certificates do not exist, with about 90 per cent of births in no official register.

How the record is made. Births may be declared at civil registration or identification offices within 45 days, which the World Bank said in May 2026 is uncommon in practice.

Last twelve months. On 24 July 2026 the government announced plans for a digital system recording births, deaths, marriages and divorces. On 31 July the Directorate was reported to be planning to link civil registration with the national ID system, with births declared from health facilities. At the handover of 10 August 2026 the outgoing director-general cited a memorandum of understanding, signed in Nairobi, for an integrated civil registration system.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The World Bank's May 2026 diagnostic lists the Directorate's civil registration system as planned only and describes no office registering digitally.

Not held. No design, procurement, pilot office or start date for a digital system is described, and whether the birth-registration pilot in Juba is digital is not stated. No dated statement that local offices register on paper is held, and the sources do not agree on whether a costed plan is in force.

STP.short: Births are entered directly in the national database at maternities, as of 2026; the share of local offices doing so is not known.
STP.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Direcção Geral dos Registos e do Notariado, an autonomous body within the justice ministry, is responsible for civil registration and developed its system with its own technicians, while the University of Aveiro in Portugal maintains and hosts it, the World Bank said in 2023. The same report found no strategic plan specifically for civil registration and identification.

Events registered digitally. The chief conservator of the civil registry said in March 2026 that births are registered by entering the data directly into the directorate's database. The World Bank said in 2023 that the system the directorate calls SIGA, implemented by 2018, registers births, deaths and marriages.

How the record is made. At the maternities the directorate's technicians and trained nurse-midwives make the registration directly in the system, on computers and printers there, the chief conservator said in March 2026. In the directorate's centres registration is done digitally, connected to servers hosted in Portugal, the World Bank said in 2023.

Last twelve months. In March 2026 the chief conservator said the directorate is eliminating paper by registering births directly from the maternities.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The chief conservator said in March 2026 that registration is done in all the country's maternities. The World Bank in 2023 counted 11 centres for all civil registration services and seven birth registration posts in maternities.

Not held. No share or count of the local offices entering records is published, and nothing says where deaths are entered. No finance fact from the last three years is held, and no current plan for civil registration.

SWZ.short: Births and deaths were entered in the national register at 14 service centres in 2022; the total number of offices is not known.
SWZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Civil Registration Department of the Ministry of Home Affairs manages the system, and the register was developed in-house with the government's National Data Centre, which hosts it. A CRVS Strategic Plan 2022-26 was launched in 2022. The World Bank's appraisal of 8 June 2026 allots US$5.5 million to digital ID and civil registration.

Events registered digitally. Births and deaths are captured into the National Population Register on registration, with 47,524 birth and 5,968 death registrations in 2022.

How the record is made. The Central Statistical Office's report for 2022 says the registration officer fills the form by hand and a typist enters it into the register, which the service centres reach over a wide-area network, the registration being complete only once it is in the system.

Last twelve months. The World Bank appraised the Digital Eswatini Project on 8 June 2026, to upgrade the existing ID and civil registration systems. Its document says paper birth and death records are stored locally without centralised backups.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Central Statistical Office's 2022 report lists 14 civil registration service centres with births and deaths registered in the register that year. The Ministry of Home Affairs' report for 2024/25 gives 15 service centres and 5 hospital registration points. In answers collected from October 2022 to April 2023, Eswatini told an AfDB and COMESA assessment that entry of vital events is electronic in all its civil registration offices.

Not held. No total of local offices is held for 2022, so the 14 centres are a count without a denominator, and no rural share or office figure from the last two years is held. The World Bank's June 2026 account of civil records on paper is not reconciled with the 2022 and 2023 accounts of electronic entry.

SYC.short: A computerised record of vital events was kept beside the manual register in 2018; where it is entered is not known.
SYC.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Civil Status Act as in force on 1 November 2022 makes the Chief Officer of Civil Status, appointed by the President and answering to the Minister responsible for civil status, keeper of the registers of births and deaths.

Events registered digitally. A contributed article in Seychelles Nation of 10 August 2018 states that the Civil Status records were computerised in 1989, and that a computerised record of vital events is kept beside the manual register and updated daily from the occurrences the Civil Status registers.

How the record is made. The Act as in force on 1 November 2022 prescribes the registers as numbered pages kept in duplicate, and its section 107A lets the Chief Officer accept statements, forms and signatures through an electronic medium.

Last twelve months. The Civil Status (Amendment) Act 2021 was assented to on 4 November 2021, to commence on a date the Minister appoints by Gazette notice.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Act as in force on 1 November 2022 provides a Central Civil Status Office in Victoria and offices at Praslin, La Digue and Anse Royale.

Not held. Where the computerised record is entered, at the offices at Praslin, La Digue and Anse Royale or centrally, and how many local offices enter it. Nothing dated after 1 November 2022 on governance or on change in the last twelve months.

TCD.short: Births were registered digitally at 97 hospital registry points in 2025; the total of local offices is not known.
TCD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The World Bank states that Chad created ANATS in 2016 as the government institution in charge of operationalising the civil registry. ANATS's director general said in November 2023 that digital birth registration follows the validated roadmap for universal birth registration by 2030. Kiosks for birth registration in eleven N'Djamena health centres were being set up with UNICEF support and EU funding in September 2024.

Events registered digitally. ANATS's coordinator of civil registration said in an account published in June 2025 that more than 120,000 children had been registered through hospital-based registry offices since 2023.

How the record is made. The World Bank stated in 2023 that civil registration officers in six hospitals enter the declaration in a mobile application ANATS calls TASDJIL, after which ANATS issues the birth certificate electronically. In the June 2025 account all data is sent by SMS to the national agency, which validates it and returns it for issuance. On 23 September 2026 the N'Djamena town hall cited the still heavy recourse to physical procedures in its civil-status service.

Last twelve months. On 23 September 2026 the commune of N'Djamena launched a project to digitise its civil registry and signed a memorandum with ANATS; an integrated management platform is planned.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The June 2025 account gives 97 digitised hospital-based civil registration points, which the government plans to raise to 600.

Not held. No total of local offices is given beside the 97 hospital points, so no share of offices is established, and nothing says deaths are registered digitally. That the entry is made at the office is said only of six hospitals in 2023.

TGO.short: A digital birth registration platform was piloted at one town hall in 2024; whether other offices register on it is not known.
TGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. WHO's Togo office reports that a national diagnostic of the birth and death registration system in 2024 produced a national roadmap for the digitalisation of civil registration and vital statistics and a multisectoral task force. UNDP Togo states that in 2024 it supported the development, deployment and operation of the digital birth registration platform.

Events registered digitally. UNDP Togo's annual report for 2024 states that the platform, in its pilot phase at the Golfe 3 town hall, simplified the registration of births and of other civil status acts. On 27 May 2021 UNDP described an application the commune of Lacs 1 calls Kadodo as recording births, deaths and marriages.

How the record is made. WHO's assessment summary for Togo, on data from 2013 to 2018, records the exchange of civil registration data from local to regional and central offices as a paper-based system.

Last twelve months. The territorial administration ministry launched the re-reading of law 2009-010 on the organisation of civil status on 21 August 2026, with support from the OIF and UNECA, and reform proposals are expected before the end of 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. UNDP Togo states that in 2024 the platform ran in its pilot phase at one town hall, Golfe 3, and that the civil status centres of the 16 communes of the Savanes region were digitised and trained to use it.

Not held. How the record is made on the digital birth registration platform, and whether the 16 Savanes communes register on it. No total of offices is given beside them, and the roadmap's period is not stated.

TUN.short: Registrars enter births and deaths into the national database after the paper register, all offices connected in 2020; how many register is not known.
TUN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Births and deaths in the civil register come under the Ministry of Interior, on a 2025 country report. The agreement to rebuild the platform, signed on 19 March 2021, was financed by the African Development Bank and falls under the national plan Tunisie Digitale 2020.

Events registered digitally. The national civil status system, which Tunisia calls Madania, holds births and deaths as well as marriages and divorces in a centralised database, on a 2025 report. It held 18.53 million birth acts and 4.14 million death acts as of 2018.

How the record is made. The registrar writes each event by hand in the paper register and then records it directly in the central database, where it is available nationwide the next morning, on a 2020 account.

Last twelve months. On 20 November, 4 December and 11 December 2025 workshops trained civil status officers and heads of municipal districts from 72 municipalities on the system, organised by the Ministry of the Interior and the National Institute of Health.

Local offices doing the digital entry. All civil registration offices have interconnected computer systems and all municipalities have access to Madania, an IDRC chapter of 2020 states, counting 350 principal offices and 170 subsidiary offices, annexes and mobile units.

Not held. No source gives the share or the number of offices that make the entry in Madania. Nothing on how the record is made or on offices is dated after 2020, and no plan or finance fact later than 2021 is held.

TZA.short: In 2024 57% of mainland registration centres were active, entering births by phone; capped because a current plan or domestic finance is not known.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. On the mainland the Registration Insolvency and Trusteeship Agency (RITA), the statutory registrar of births and deaths, introduced the Civil Registration System in 2017 and runs it. Its Strategic Plan for 2021/22 to 2025/26 names that system for all its birth and death registration. For 2018/19 RITA reported a treasury allocation of USD 510,768 against a requirement of USD 27.5 million.

Events registered digitally. RITA's platform, which it calls e-RITA, registers births, deaths, marriages, divorces and adoptions, on its 2025 presentation. The system held 18,464,255 births as of September 2024 and 977,761 deaths registered since 2017.

How the record is made. At the under-five registration centres, which are ward offices and health facilities, officers record a birth by hand in a register and then enter the same details into the online system by phone, the national audit found in October 2024.

Last twelve months. Zanzibar's registration agency reported a 2025/2026 improvement of its system, with streamlined workflows and a unified mobile app. On the mainland RITA extended its system to all districts in October 2024.

Local offices doing the digital entry. RITA's monitoring plan, as the 2024 audit reports it, counts 6,341 of 11,053 under-five registration centres as active, 57 per cent of them. In Zanzibar the agency states in 2026 that registration runs on its own platform in all 11 districts.

Not held. The 57 per cent is centres RITA counts as active, not a count of centres entering digitally, and no later figure gives a total; Zanzibar's offices are not counted. No domestic finance fact later than 2018/19 and no plan running past June 2026 is held for the mainland system.

UGA.short: District offices enter births and deaths into the central register, in most districts in 2020; how many offices do so is not known.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA), under the Minister of Internal Affairs, holds all of Uganda's civil registration systems, it said on 18 July 2026. Its Strategic Plan III for 2025/26 to 2029/30 was finalised in 2025/26, and its 2026/27 budget estimate of UGX 155.948 billion is all Government of Uganda money.

Events registered digitally. NIRA's system, which it calls the Mobile Vital Records System, registered 498,439 live births and 22,182 deaths in 2024, on the statistics bureau's figures. On 18 July 2026 NIRA said it had built a births and deaths module on its identity system that issues an identity number once a birth is notified.

How the record is made. A paper notification form is entered into the web-based system at district offices and health facilities, and each entry is recorded directly in the central register, on a 2020 brief.

Last twelve months. In 2025/26 to 31 December 2025 NIRA registered 123,526 births and 9,935 deaths.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The system was used in at least 112 of 135 districts and in 222 of the 5,230 health facilities that handle births, an IDRC brief said in 2020.

Not held. No share or count of offices making the entry is held, and nothing on offices or on how the record is made is dated after 2020. The new births and deaths module is reported with no offices and no date of going live.

ZAF.short: Births are registered online at 242 equipped health facilities, as of March 2026; the share of local offices registering digitally is not known.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Department of Home Affairs itself rolls out the online birth registration system to health facilities, on its 2024/25 annual report. Its amended annual performance plan for 2025/26 targets nine health facilities and allocates R21 million to the rollout.

Events registered digitally. The department reports that its online birth registration system was available at 242 health facilities by the end of 2024/25. Its Annual Performance Plan 2026/27 schedules the digitalising of death registration for 2028/29.

How the record is made. The National Department of Health states for 2024/25 that births are registered and certificates issued at the health facility, by Home Affairs officials posted there, through an online system. Home Affairs stated in September 2025 that births are captured onto the National Population Register at local offices and health facilities from the paper Notice of Birth form.

Last twelve months. The department reported progress on online birth registration in the fourth quarter of 2025/26. The Portfolio Committee on Home Affairs reports that the 2025/26 target of automated birth registration at 47 health facilities was missed and the rollout deferred to 2026/27.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Annual Performance Plan 2026/27 counts 242 health facilities equipped with online birth registration systems, beside 325 front offices and 220 mobile offices. The National Department of Health counts 299 health facilities able to register births at the end of 2024/25, against 1,445 public health facilities with maternity wards.

Not held. No share of local offices registering births digitally is held: the counts are of health facilities equipped, and how the front offices make the record is not described. No digital registration of deaths is held, and no figure for the last year's progress.

ZMB.short: Births are registered in a national system deployed in eleven districts in 2026; how many local offices enter records themselves is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security describes the Integrated National Registration Information System, INRIS, as the ministry's national and civil registration management system, run through the Department of National Registration, Passport and Citizenship, in a 2026 statement to the National Assembly. The Eighth National Development Plan 2022-2026 commits the Government to operationalise it. The Minister puts the cost of the exercise at K1,069,366,200.

Events registered digitally. The Minister states that enrolment has commenced in the INRIS districts, including registration of births and issuance of birth certificates using the system. The ministry said in December 2025 that about 1.3 million citizens have been enrolled on INRIS and over 500,000 births and deaths registered.

How the record is made. A preprint of September 2025 states that the department runs a paper-based system for birth and death registration, and that completed death notification forms are carried weekly from local offices to provincial or national headquarters for entry into INRIS. The Lavushimanda district officer said in September 2026 that the district office is implementing digital civil registration through INRIS.

Last twelve months. The Lavushimanda district office registered over 3,000 children under five in the four months to September 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Minister's 2026 statement has INRIS deployed in eleven districts. A CDC Foundation case study of 2025 says the expansion of INRIS has brought access to civil registration services to 81 of 116 districts.

Not held. No count of local offices that enter events in INRIS themselves is held, and the accounts differ on whether entry is made at the office or at provincial or national headquarters. No source of funds is stated for the current exercise, and nothing dated in the last twelve months shows a national advance or retreat.

ZWE.short: Births are entered digitally at computerised offices; at least 93 of 282 offices were computerised in 2026, and how many register digitally is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Registrar General's department presents the computerisation of its provinces, districts and sub-offices as its own decentralisation programme, in July 2026. UNICEF says Zimbabwe developed a strategic action plan for civil registration and vital statistics for 2023-2027. The Appropriation (2026) Act appropriated ZiG 1,470,460,000 to the Civil Registration programme, and the ten sub-offices announced in August 2026 are funded by China and delivered by UNICEF.

Events registered digitally. UNICEF Zimbabwe stated in July 2025 that at the computerised sub-office at Mpilo Hospital mothers register newborns and obtain a birth certificate before discharge.

How the record is made. UNICEF Zimbabwe stated in July 2025 that the computerised registry offices and sub-offices allow real-time data entry at the office. UNICEF's chief of child protection said on 7 August 2026 that some decentralised sub-offices are not computerised.

Last twelve months. In October 2025 the Minister of Home Affairs and Cultural Heritage announced plans to computerise sub-offices across the country. On 7 August 2026 UNICEF and the government announced a China-funded project to computerise, digitalise and solar-power 10 sub-offices in eight districts.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The Deputy Registrar General said on 22 July 2026 that all 10 provinces and 63 districts have been computerised and more than 20 of 209 sub-offices. UNICEF Zimbabwe named, in July 2025, digital registration as operational at Mpilo Hospital, Kariangwe in Binga, Bubi, Manama Mission Hospital, Mahusekwa, Murambinda and Epworth.

Not held. No count of offices registering births digitally is held: the Registrar General's count is of offices computerised, and what a computerised office does is not stated. Where the digital record is held is not known, and no digital entry of deaths is held.

AGO.short: Schools answered a twice-yearly school count questionnaire in 2021/22; whether any primary school keeps a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
AGO.summary: Not held. No dated statement says whether primary schools keep their pupils' records on paper, and nothing held describes a system with a record for each pupil that a school adds to during the year.

BDI.short: In 2023 the yearly school count was collected on paper; whether primary schools keep per-pupil records is not known, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not held. No dated statement says whether primary schools keep their pupils' records on paper, and nothing held describes a system with a record for each pupil that a school adds to during the year.

BEN.short: Primary schools entered enrolments and class lists themselves in 2026; how many do, and whether any enter attendance or results, is not known.
BEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Minister of Nursery and Primary Education, in a letter of 16 February 2026, calls EDUCMASTER a management tool for the sub-sector and orders its use by his departmental directors, district heads and school heads. The government's progress report of December 2020 presents the system, which it calls the SIGE, as a reform of its own action programme.

Levels in use. The December 2020 report says use of the SIGE, which it also calls Educmaster, is compulsory in all public and private pre-primary, primary, secondary and technical schools. La Nation reported a public primary school head in Cotonou entering her pupils on 18 December 2024.

How the record is kept. The minister's letter of February 2026 says schools themselves enter enrolments and update class lists. In secondary schools, the ministry's information systems director said in December 2024, collèges and lycées enter enrolments, transfers and absences and load each pupil's end-of-semester averages.

Last twelve months. On 16 February 2026 the minister ordered every school to complete its enrolments for all nursery and primary classes by 23 February, with heads of schools that did not to be barred from examination work in June 2026. In July 2026 the Conseil National de l'Éducation recommended following up that heads of secondary establishments record girls' enrolment exhaustively.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The letter of February 2026 says several schools enter only their final-year examination candidates and leave the other nursery and primary classes not updated.

Not held. No number or share of primary schools entering data is published, and nothing shows primary schools entering attendance or results during the year. How the system is paid for is not stated, and no current plan naming it is held.

BFA.short: A national pupil register was in pilot in 2024 and enrolment had not begun by June 2025; the number of schools is not known.
BFA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The education ministry's statistics directorate issued the pilot-phase report on FIUE-BF, its name for a national file of pupils with unique identification, in February 2024. On 25 June 2025 the ministers of digital transition and basic education reviewed the national pupil file their technical teams are building, with technical and financial support from the WURI project. The World Bank's appraisal of 14 April 2025 finances a student management platform from IDA and the Global Partnership for Education.

Levels in use. At 25 June 2025 the national platform was meant to follow pupils from primary school to university, and enrolment had not begun.

How the record is kept. LuxDev states that in 2023 the establishments in the FIUE-BF pilot handled enrolment, the publication of school results and school identity cards online. The World Bank's appraisal of 14 April 2025 states that key education data are stored mainly as hard copies.

Last twelve months. LuxDev's project page shows the programme that supported tracking each pupil by a unique identifier as closed, having run from 4 May 2018 to 31 December 2025.

Primary schools doing the digital input. In February 2024 FIUE-BF was at its pilot phase, with generalisation still ahead. At 14 April 2025 the student management platform, with a smartphone application for schools, was still to be designed, and at 25 June 2025 progressive enrolment of pupils was due to start at the next school year.

Not held. The number of pilot establishments, and whether they are primary or secondary, is not held, and no source reports the pupil file past its pilot. No current plan naming the system is held, nor whether results are entered during the school year.

BWA.short: A fund was connecting remote primary schools to broadband in 2024; how schools keep pupil records is not known, so no stage is set.
BWA.summary: Not held. No dated statement of how primary schools keep their learners' records is held. No system holding a record per learner is described.

CAF.short: By 2026 the ministry ran a yearly school count; whether schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. No dated statement of how primary schools keep their learners' records is held. No system holding a record per learner is described.

CIV.short: A per-pupil performance record started in five Abidjan pilot schools, level not named, in January 2024; whether it went further is not known.
CIV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The education ministry's national strategy for digitalising education, covering 2024 to 2028, names the project it calls DOBCONNECT among the achievements it builds on and carries a budgeted action matrix. The vendor's 2019 page for the platform named SMART ECOLE says it was designed for the ministry by its information systems directorate and is run by its schools directorate.

Levels in use. SMART ECOLE's page invites pupils of nursery schools, primary schools, lycées and collèges to identify themselves online for school year 2019-2020.

How the record is kept. The strategy says DOBCONNECT collects information on pupils' school performance so that each can be followed individually, from January 2024 in its pilot establishments. SMART ECOLE, by its 2019 page, manages schools from online enrolment to the proclamation of school results.

Last twelve months. The strategy gave DOBCONNECT's general rollout as due in May 2024.

Primary schools doing the digital input. DOBCONNECT was started in January 2024 in 5 pilot establishments of the Abidjan regional directorates, the strategy says.

Not held. Nothing shows DOBCONNECT beyond its five pilot establishments, their level, or who enters its data, and no count of schools using SMART ECOLE is held. No source of finance is held, and nothing dated in the last twelve months.

CMR.short: How primary schools keep their pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
CMR.summary: Not held. No source held says how primary schools keep their learners' records, on paper or digitally. The education systems named for Cameroon are held by name only, with nothing on what they do in schools.

COD.short: Ministry staff, not schools, registered pupils by app in a 20-primary-school pilot in April 2026; whether it will go national is not known.
COD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A Corus International article of 4 August 2026 by the director of SERNIE, the education ministry's service for individual learner data, states that ownership and use of the system it calls EDUSER rest with the ministry, operated by SERNIE with technical support from CGA Technologies. It says the pilot was funded and its future is uncertain without continued investment.

Levels in use. The April 2026 pilot of EDUSER was run in 20 primary schools of Kasai province.

How the record is kept. SERNIE's director writes that since 1991 its staff have recorded learners in schools on paper forms carried to Kinshasa for central data entry. Under EDUSER, SERNIE staff on their usual school visits register each learner by app, replacing the paper forms.

Last twelve months. In April 2026 SERNIE completed the first test of EDUSER in schools, a three-week pilot, after training its staff at national, provincial and local levels. The director says it laid the basis for a national rollout, which is not funded.

Primary schools doing the digital input. SERNIE teams registered 8,634 learners in 20 primary schools of Kasai province in the three weeks, which the director calls only a pilot phase.

Not held. No primary school is shown entering its own learners' records, and no national count or share of schools is held. No plan naming EDUSER is held, nor who funded the pilot.

COG.short: A November 2023 decree creates a per-pupil record that schools are to fill; whether any school uses it is not known.
COG.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Decree 2023-1751 of 2 November 2023 creates an education management information system, which Congo calls the SIGE, inside the ministry of preschool, primary and secondary education and literacy. The ministry's information systems directorate administers it and the state agency ACSI maintains it. The decree finances it in public schools from the State budget, gifts and partners, and names no amount.

Levels in use. No level uses a school-level system. In May 2023 a digital workspace for primary and secondary schools, the ENT, existed only as a specification written for the ministry by a consultant of the AUF's APPRENDRE programme.

How the record is kept. The decree assigns data entry to the schools or their inspectorates: each learner registered under a unique number, with grades, report cards and school record books digitised.

Last twelve months. The decree creating the system is dated 2 November 2023.

Primary schools doing the digital input. None. The May 2023 specification proposed a trial from September 2023 in a few schools to be chosen by the ministry, for example two primary schools and one secondary.

Not held. Whether staff were trained, equipment delivered or any school took part in a trial. How schools keep their learners' records, and anything dated after the decree of 2 November 2023.

COM.short: Schools have entered marks since June 2025, and 45% of public primary schools were integrated by February 2026; the share entering marks is not known.
COM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of National Education supervises e-Msomo, validates its data and authorises the printing of report cards, its deputy secretary general said on 25 November 2025. The digital agency ANADEN places the platform within the Comores Numérique 2028 strategy. In June 2025 it was reported as funded by UNICEF.

Levels in use. Primary and secondary. At 2 February 2026 the ministry counted all public secondary schools and 45% of public primary schools as integrated into e-Msomo.

How the record is kept. School heads enrol pupils and generate report cards, and teachers log in to enter marks that cannot be changed afterwards; each pupil gets a school identification number (November 2025). In February 2026 schools' administrative teams were entering pupil lists, teacher lists and marks statements.

Last twelve months. By 25 November 2025 the ministry gave registration as 100% in Ngazidja and Mwali and 65% in Ndzuwani. On 2 February 2026 it gave late schools one more week and announced that the platform's single report card will be the only document accepted for university enrolment.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The ministry's secretary general put the rate of integration into e-Msomo at 45% of public primary schools on 2 February 2026. It is a rate of schools integrated.

Not held. The number of schools behind the 45%, the share of primary schools entering marks, and any figure for private primary schools. Whether a national plan names e-Msomo, and any domestic finance for it.

CPV.short: Teachers must record pupils' absences and marks in a system put in all 395 basic schools by 2019; the share entering them is not known.
CPV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Education's school management system, SIGE, was created by the state agency NOSi in partnership with the ministry. The Plano Estratégico da Educação 2022-2026 names it throughout and costs 3 million escudos to extend it to pre-school and private schools. In July 2025 the national director of education named UNICEF as main funder of a new special-needs module.

Levels in use. Primary and secondary. The ministry states that SIGE was completed in all 43 secondary schools in July 2018 and in basic education schools in February 2019. A ministerial order obliges every school, public, semi-public and private, to adopt it from 1 September 2025.

How the record is kept. The ministry's guidance for 2023/2024 requires teachers to record absences daily in SIGE's digital class register and to enter each assessment within 15 days. Since June 2025 the eSkola app shows parents each pupil's marks and absences from SIGE in real time.

Last twelve months. The order for the 2025/2026 school year, in force from 1 September 2025, requires teachers to record pupils' assessment on SIGE's result-entry sheets.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The ministry states that SIGE was implemented in all 395 basic education schools by February 2019, a count of schools where it was implemented. On 25 June 2025 the government said it was already used in all basic and secondary schools.

Not held. A published share or count of basic education schools entering attendance or marks, and any share for rural schools. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months, and the donor finance stated is for one module only.

DJI.short: In 2023 school heads registered pupils and sent absences through a national per-pupil record; the share of primary schools doing so is not known.
DJI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The education ministry developed the pupil management system it calls GOSE and, as at 28 November 2023, planned its extension. The minister's circular of 1 September 2025 makes consolidating it a priority for the 2025-2026 school year. The World Bank's September 2019 appraisal costed the data systems work at US$2.55 million, US$0.8 million from an IDA grant and US$1.75 million from a Global Partnership for Education grant.

Levels in use. As at 28 November 2023 each pupil had a unique identifier in GOSE from pre-school to senior school, the World Bank reported.

How the record is kept. At that date the school principal registered and transferred pupils in the application, and pupil and teacher absences were transmitted through it to central management. Pupils' grades and history were additions the ministry planned.

Last twelve months. In an interview of 20 November 2025 the education minister said the ministry's platforms give it reliable data to detect pupils in difficulty before they drop out, and that more than 3,000 pupils had been supported through the system.

Primary schools doing the digital input. All public schools transmitted their data through GOSE as at 28 November 2023, the World Bank reported, with the rollout in phases and refugee and private schools to follow. The project's measure of primary schools transmitting on time, with a target of 70 per cent of public and 50 per cent of private schools, was still unmet at that date.

Not held. No share of primary schools entering absences, nor a count with its total, and no figure for rural schools. Nothing dated after 2023 says how many schools use the system, and the 2025-2026 priority rests on a circular, not a costed plan.

DZA.short: It is not known whether primary schools keep pupil records on paper or in a system, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: Not held. Whether primary schools keep their pupils' records on paper or in a system, at which levels, and in how many schools. Nothing held says who runs or pays for such a system.

EGY.short: The ministry's 2023-2027 plan is to build a per-pupil record; whether primary schools use one is not known, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: Not held. At which levels a system of pupil records is in use, how the record is kept and how many primary schools enter data. How the planned system is financed is not stated, and nothing dated in the past twelve months is held.

ERI.short: A digital platform for the yearly school count was built by 2026; how schools keep pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. No dated statement that primary schools keep their learners' records on paper is held. Nothing is held on any system that keeps a record for each learner.

ETH.short: The ministry's web-based system, with a number for each pupil, was piloted by June 2025; whether any primary school uses it is not known.
ETH.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Education developed and completed its web-based EMIS and finalised a directive for it, with World Bank support, by June 2025. It was built under a Global Partnership for Education grant through the World Bank. The ministry's sector plan for 2020/21 to 2024/25 planned a student database and a digital application for schools to report pupils' daily data.

Levels in use. At June 2025 the system covered federal, regional, woreda and school levels, and deployment to 4,500 primary schools in 156 weredas was planned for July 2025 to June 2026.

How the record is kept. The system gives unique identification numbers to students, teachers and schools, as reported at June 2025. A UNESCO-commissioned case study researched in late 2019 found that schools keep registers on paper and collect attendance without storing it centrally.

Last twelve months. In November 2025 UNICEF partnered with HISP Ethiopia and the HISP Centre to assist the ministry and regional education bureaus on DHIS2 for Education, working with schools in four regions, where tools to collect learning outcomes and student attendance were still to be developed.

Primary schools doing the digital input. UNICEF, the grant agent, reports that by June 2025 the digitised system had been finalised and piloted, with deployment to primary schools not begun; the tender for 4,500 primary-school computers was set for August 2025. The sector plan published in 2021 gave a baseline of none for a student database and zero institutions networked.

Not held. Nothing shows the web-based system in live use in a primary school: no source dated after June 2025 reports the planned deployment. The number of pilot schools, the levels piloted and what the piloted system records are not stated.

GAB.short: 728 schools managed pupils' marks in a vendor's application in 2024; the share of primary schools is not known, as no total is given.
GAB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The learner identification is run by SOSUP, a state body, and announced by the ministry's Secretary-General as compulsory, on 4 November 2025. Xgest belongs to the start-up Groupe Tereza, with the State its client, as at 27 September 2024. On 24 September 2024 the ministry closed pupil enrolment on X-Gest after irregularities and ordered that no personal data pass through it.

Levels in use. The identification for 2025/2026 covers public and private pre-primary, primary and secondary schools, the Secretary-General stated on 4 November 2025. The World Bank's 2019 diagnostic put X-Gest in 92 secondary schools, expanding to the remaining secondary schools and to primary schools.

How the record is kept. Schools managed pupils' numbers and marks and published results in Xgest, on Gabonreview's account of 27 September 2024, and enrolments and re-enrolments for 2024-2025 were made on it. The 2025/2026 identification is made online once for the school year.

Last twelve months. On 4 November 2025 the ministry opened a second phase of school identification, announced the online learner identification for 2025/2026 and barred pupils of unidentified schools from it. Focus Groupe Media reported in March 2026 that SOSUP had been deploying eFormation, giving every establishment and every pupil a unique identifier.

Primary schools doing the digital input. Gabonreview reported on 27 September 2024 that Xgest is used by 728 schools, a count of schools of all levels together. The ministry posts the list of schools registered for the identification on SOSUP's site.

Not held. The 728 schools come with no total and no level of schooling, so no share of primary schools is held. Whether the school or the family makes the yearly identification entry, how many schools are in the register, and any plan or budget for either system are not stated.

GHA.short: In November 2025, 733 primary schools reported each pupil's literacy and numeracy results on a digital platform; their share of primary schools is not known.
GHA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Schools reporting on what the World Bank calls the DL+ Platform is a condition carrying US$25 million under a project financing that is grant-financed by GPE, SCALE funders and the Early Learning Partnership and had disbursed nothing by November 2025.

Levels in use. The programme whose results schools report on the platform is for lower and upper primary, the World Bank said in November 2025. Senior high schools upload student records to the examinations council's Student Transcript Portal, live since 2024.

How the record is kept. Primary schools assess and report literacy and numeracy outcomes for individual learners on the platform. Secondary schools have uploaded over 60 million academic records since 2024, at a 97.2% national average completion rate, with completion reviewed monthly by regional and national committees.

Last twelve months. The count of schools reporting on the platform stood at 733 in August 2024, in June 2025 and in November 2025. The World Bank says the training of teachers to start reporting was delayed by the finance ministry's disbursement cap, in force from January 2025.

Primary schools doing the digital input. By the World Bank's count, 733 schools were reporting on the platform at 27 November 2025, against a target of 16,000 by December 2028.

Not held. No total of primary schools is given beside the 733, so their share of all primary schools is not known. Nor is it stated how often a school reports, who owns the platform or whether a current plan names it.

GIN.short: In March 2026 a nationwide registration gave primary pupils a single school number, in secondary since 2022; how many schools took part is not known.
GIN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Pre-University Education instituted the unique pupil number it calls the matricule unique, within a digitalisation run by its examinations directorate, which also coordinates training on the registration platform. A roadmap validated on 2 November 2021 provides for a single integrated system whose pupil module covers attendance, class assessments and examination results.

Levels in use. The matricule began in 2022 at collège and lycée and was extended to primary in a nationwide registration from 5 to 25 March 2026. In Labé prefecture a mission ordered on 30 March 2026 accompanied the registration of primary pupils, each photographed for the matricule.

How the record is kept. Each pupil is given one matricule in the registration, for which public and private school heads were mobilised in March 2026; transfers between schools are then detected automatically.

Last twelve months. The ministry announced the digital registration of primary pupils on 25 February 2026, with officers of the regional, prefectoral and communal education offices starting training. Registration was launched in Matoto on 5 March 2026 and ran school by school in Labé under the order of 30 March.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The March 2026 registration covered the whole national territory, public and private schools alike, by the account of Matoto's communal education director.

Not held. No number or share of primary schools registered is given, and no source says who keys the record: those trained are officers of the education offices, not school staff. No plan dated within three years and no source of finance is held.

GMB.short: Schools record each pupil in a national register, scaled up from 200 pilot schools in 2021; how many primary schools enter data is not known.
GMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The system is the Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education's, run by its own unit, as GPE KIX described it in October 2025. An October 2022 account says it was aligned to the Education Policy 2016-2030 and built with financial support from GPE-KIX and Norad.

Levels in use. A learner census run with the Gambia Bureau of Statistics collected individual-level data on children attending primary schools, DHIS2 reported in October 2022, with work continuing to extend the system to all basic and secondary schools.

How the record is kept. Schools record each learner's socio-economic background, attendance and progression in the ministry's digital student registry under a unique ID, DHIS2 reported in August 2025, with modules for daily attendance and exam results.

Last twelve months. GPE KIX in October 2025 described attendance tracking and digital school report cards in use at school level.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The registry began as a pilot in 200 schools in 2020 and the ministry scaled it to national level in 2021. By August 2025 it included nearly 80% of Gambian learners, a share of learners, by DHIS2's account.

Not held. No count or share of primary schools entering data is published, and the sources disagree on whether the school application is still a pilot. Finance within the past three years and any dated event in the last twelve months are not held.

GNB.short: The yearly school count ran on a new platform in 2025; whether schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
