GNB.summary: Not held. No record for each learner that schools add to during the year is held. No dated statement that primary schools keep learner records on paper only is held either.

GNQ.short: Schools return a yearly count by questionnaire (2026); whether any keeps a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not held. No record for each learner that schools add to during the year is held. No dated statement that primary schools keep learner records on paper only is held either.

KEN.short: Primary and secondary schools register each pupil on the national system (2026); how many primary schools do so, and any attendance entry, is not known.
KEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Education's National Education Sector Strategic Plan 2023-2027 names the Kenya Education Management Information System (KEMIS), as the ministry calls it, and carries costed yearly lines for developing it. Techweez reported in September 2026 that KEMIS is funded through the World Bank-backed Kenya Primary Education Equity in Learning Programme.

Levels in use. NEMIS, the system KEMIS replaces, covered all basic education institutions, primary and secondary, as Development Gateway and IREX reported in May 2024. KEMIS is built to hold data from early childhood education through to university, on Techweez's account of September 2026.

How the record is kept. A ministry circular published on 17 August 2026 tells schools to enter and correct each learner's record in KEMIS themselves: examination or assessment number, names, demographic details and parent or guardian identification. Schools entered pathway, subject and senior-school choices against the records of nearly 1.2 million Grade 9 learners in September 2026.

Last twelve months. KEMIS became the required platform for the 2026 Grade 10 selection, and its Learner Validation Engine was operational by August 2026. In September 2026 schools reported failed logins, slow responses and submissions that did not save. In late August 2026 the Principal Secretary told the Public Accounts Committee that the latest capitation payment used manually verified data because KEMIS was not yet complete.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The World Bank reported in March 2024 that about 60 per cent of primary school learners were registered in NEMIS.

Not held. No source describes schools entering attendance or results for each learner during the year, and no rural figure is held. No share or count of primary schools entering data is held for either system: two figures for 2021, 65 and 90 per cent, disagree and count schools that had submitted data.

LBR.short: The Ministry said in 2026 that its school data system is paper-based and a per-pupil record planned; whether any pilot has begun is not known.
LBR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Education is drafting the EMIS Policy itself. Its policy dialogue of 1 to 5 September 2025 validated a costed three-year action plan whose priorities include a national unique learner and teacher ID. The plan is for USD 4.5 million, 60 per cent from the government and 40 per cent from development partners.

Levels in use. The African Union's peer review of 1 and 2 September 2025 found unique learner and teacher IDs absent, and describes a system that reaches about 1.5 million learners in 6,500 schools through a school census.

How the record is kept. At a consultation on 28 and 29 September 2026 the Ministry's planning director described the existing system as paper-based and called for a digitised one. In September 2026 the Ministry opened a five-day session to develop and validate a record-keeping booklet for school records on students, teachers and attendance.

Last twelve months. The Ministry held the two-day consultation of September 2026 to draft, review and validate an EMIS Policy for a real-time school data system, and said a study tour for its technicians was being arranged.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The Deputy Minister for Administration said at the close of the consultation that systems at schools feeding student and teacher attendance to a central dashboard are a goal not yet reached, and that the Ministry still relies largely on periodic data collection.

Not held. Nothing shows staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot schools chosen for a school-level system or the learner ID. The Ministry's paper statement names no level and no school count, and no budget line for the plan is shown.

LBY.short: A system launched in 2024 gathers school data by online survey; how schools keep each pupil's record is not known, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not held. Nothing held says how primary schools keep their learners' records, on paper or digitally. No system held is shown to hold a record per learner that a school adds to during the year.

LSO.short: A 2018 pilot tracked individual pupils in one hundred schools; their level, and whether it still runs, is not known.
LSO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In 2018 the Ministry of Education and Training was itself implementing OpenEMIS as its new education information system. UNICEF supported the rollout, and the pilot drew on an existing World Bank project, the Lesotho Basic Education Improvement Project.

Levels in use. The 2018 pilot was set in one hundred low-performance schools, according to Development Gateway's diagnostic for UNICEF Lesotho.

How the record is kept. The pilot tracked individual learners in those schools, under OpenEMIS, the platform the Ministry was adopting that year.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is from 2018, when, with UNICEF supporting it, the rollout was beginning with the pilot.

Primary schools doing the digital input. Development Gateway reported in 2018 that one hundred schools were in the pilot, a count of pilot schools and not a share of all primary schools.

Not held. The level of the pilot schools and who entered the records are not stated, and nothing dated since 2018 shows whether the pilot still runs or went further. No current plan or domestic budget for a per-learner system is held.

MAR.short: Every school has registered its pupils in a national per-pupil record since 2014; how many primary schools enter attendance or marks is not known.
MAR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. MASSAR was developed by the Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training and launched at the end of 2013, the World Bank's identity diagnostic states. On 7 May 2026 the ministry's secretary-general instructed the regional academies on who records and who validates absence in 'Massar+ Idara'.

Levels in use. In May 2014 MASSAR's register covered every child aged 6 to 18 enrolled in any national educational establishment, 6,512,192 pupils, by the same diagnostic. The national evaluation body's atlas of 2019 follows cohorts of primary pupils into lower secondary from MASSAR's individual records for 2014 to 2018.

How the record is kept. In June 2014 each establishment registered and vetted its own pupils into a central database, and each pupil kept one number for the whole of their schooling. By the 2019 atlas MASSAR has a pupil assessment component through which parents consult their children's marks online. In the pioneer middle schools, by the ministry's letter of 7 May 2026, teachers record absence at the start of each lesson and the school administration keys it into 'Massar+ Idara'.

Last twelve months. The letter of 7 May 2026 rolls out a new digital component for daily monitoring of pupil absence in the pioneer middle schools.

Primary schools doing the digital input. In June 2014 pupils were vetted at each of the country's 10,000 learning establishments, the World Bank's diagnostic states: a figure for schools of all levels registering pupils.

Not held. No share or count of primary schools entering attendance or results is held, and daily entry is shown for lower secondary schools only. Who keys primary pupils' marks, and the plan and financing, are not held.

MDG.short: A pilot gave 180,000 pupils in one district a permanent number in 2026; whether any primary school beyond the pilot has enrolled is not known.
MDG.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The digital enrolment of learners is carried out by the Ministry of National Education and the Unité de gouvernance digitale, within the PRODIGY project, by the report of its launch on 11 May 2026. The World Bank's mission of December 2025 counted its field activities among the items to draw down the remaining funds of the Bank-financed PRODIGY project before 30 June 2026.

Levels in use. The Numéro Unique d'Identification Scolaire, as the ministry names it, gives each learner a permanent identifier from pre-school to lycée, in public and private establishments, the ministry said in May 2026.

How the record is kept. Learners are enrolled digitally, once, to receive the identifier, in an operation of May 2026.

Last twelve months. In December 2025 the enrolment's field activities were still to be carried out, the World Bank's mission recorded. On 11 May 2026 the scale-up was launched at a public lower-secondary school in Ambatolampy district, with a ministry target of 4.2 million learners from 19,303 establishments in 48 school districts by 12 June 2026.

Primary schools doing the digital input. Between March and April 2026 the pilot in the Atsimondrano school district enrolled 180,000 learners from 792 public and private establishments of all levels, by the report of May 2026: a figure for schools covered by the enrolment.

Not held. No total of establishments in the pilot district and no separate count of primary schools is held, and for the scale-up only the target is held, not a result. Who keys the record and any plan are not held.

MLI.short: A donor project gave families cards for heads to scan pupils' attendance on tablets in 2020; whether any school does so is not known.
MLI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In February 2020 the PAIS project was a partnership of UNICEF, the World Food Programme, the International Rescue Committee and the Norwegian Refugee Council, UNICEF Mali states, and was funded by the European Union.

Levels in use. UNICEF Mali, in February 2020, describes the scheme at the Kénèkolo village school, in a passage on children aged seven to twelve missing primary education.

How the record is kept. Under PAIS each family in the target areas holds an electronic card with each child registered on it, which the school principal scans onto a tablet as children attend, to take attendance and make it available to the Ministry of Education, by UNICEF Mali in February 2020.

Last twelve months. In February 2020 UNICEF Mali said the Kénèkolo school would digitise its attendance system that year.

Primary schools doing the digital input. By February 2020 families in the target areas of Kayes, Koulikoro, Ségou and Sikasso had been given cards, UNICEF Mali states, naming the one school.

Not held. Nothing is held since February 2020, so who runs and pays for the scheme now and any event in the last twelve months are not held. No count or share of schools scanning attendance is held, and no school is named as doing so.

MOZ.short: A pilot tracking individual pupils was reported in 2025; which schools, how many and whether it has gone further is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The education ministry's Plano Tecnológico da Educação of May 2019, with targets for 2020-2025, names the ministry as responsible for designing the academic information system it calls SEGI, with provincial directorates, district services and schools implementing it. The plan costs the programme at 39.36 million meticais a year.

Levels in use. The 2019 plan's first-phase target was for 100% of secondary and 10% of primary schools to take part in SEGI.

How the record is kept. The policy brief on the KIX Africa 19 knowledge café of 22 July 2025 states that the ministry's statistics system, StatEduc, is fed by censuses on physical questionnaires and holds data aggregated by class, subject and gender, not individual student records.

Last twelve months. GPE KIX reported on 21 August 2026 that the collection of education data at school level is largely paper-based.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The KIX brief of July 2025 recommends mandating individual student tracking "as piloted in Mozambique".

Not held. The pilot of individual student tracking is named with no system, level, number of schools or method of entry, and nothing says it has gone past its pilot. No ownership, plan or financing dated within the last three years is held.

MRT.short: Pupil registration for 2026-2027 opened on a ministry platform in September 2026; who enters the records and in how many schools is not known.
MRT.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Tefassil reported on 28 September 2026 that the registration and transfer of pupils through the platform the ministry calls Siraj runs to a timetable set by the Ministry of Education and Reform of the Education System. The state news agency reported on 3 June 2025 that a ministerial committee chaired by the Prime Minister follows the system.

Levels in use. On 28 April 2025 education inspectors and heads of service of the Brakna regional directorate were trained on the system. Radio Mauritanie reported on 12 June 2026 that district inspectors and the heads of the beneficiary schools in Trarza are to update data through it.

How the record is kept. Registration, transfers and corrections of pupils' status for the 2026-2027 school year go through Siraj, open from 28 September to 20 October 2026.

Last twelve months. Pupil registration for 2026-2027 opened through Siraj on 28 September 2026, the ministry urging parents to register their children early.

Primary schools doing the digital input. Tefassil's report of 28 September 2026 presents Siraj as the channel for registering and transferring pupils for 2026-2027.

Not held. Whether pupil registration through Siraj is a pilot or in full use, whether the school or the parent enters the record, which level of schooling it covers and how many schools use it are not held. No plan or financing is stated.

MUS.short: A per-pupil school record system was being designed in 2019; whether it was built or any school uses it is not known.
MUS.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. UNESCO IITE reported after a mission of 11-15 February 2019 that the system is the Ministry of Education's to establish, coordinated by its Director of E-Education with UNESCO technical support, and that the needs assessment and design reports were to support including its resource needs in the 2019/2020 budget.

Levels in use. In February 2019 the system was planned for national, zone and school levels, from pre-primary to tertiary.

How the record is kept. The 2019 mission set out to design a school integrated management information system that is to track each student's progress, including classroom assessment.

Last twelve months. The education ministry's indicative procurement plan for financial year 2026-2027, dated 17 August 2026, names an EMIS.

Primary schools doing the digital input. In February 2019 the system was still to be developed, over twelve months following a three-month technical document.

Not held. Nothing dated since February 2019 says whether the system was built, piloted or used in any school, at which level, or how pupils' records are kept. No ownership, plan or financing dated within the last three years is held.

MWI.short: Schools kept each pupil's record in paper registers made by hand in 2026; whether any digital record is being prepared is not known.
MWI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Cohort tracking, which gives each pupil a Learner Identification Number on entry to school, is the Ministry of Education's, and sits inside what the country calls its Education Management Information System.

Levels in use. Cohort tracking passes from schools to zonal and district officers.

How the record is kept. On paper. A May 2026 policy brief from the Unlocking Data Initiative says cohort tracking rests on paper records and several manual registers: class attendance and performance, master enrolment, and admission.

Last twelve months. Nothing moved. The same brief says the cohort tracking data has rarely been analysed since 2012 and is difficult to use for planning, and in May 2026 digitising it was a recommendation.

Primary schools doing the digital input. Schools make the registers themselves, by hand, as of May 2026.

Not held. Nothing held names a school level, a count of schools, or an owner, plan or budget for a digital record of each pupil. No preparation or pilot of one for primary schools is on record.

NAM.short: In 2018, 807 of 1,848 schools were connected to the national school system and 103 piloted daily attendance entry; anything since is not known.
NAM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. School-Link, an EDUPAC product, came to the Ministry of Education, Arts and Culture in 2013, was approved as the national system for all schools and is offered to them free, with a helpdesk in the ministry's ICT division. The 2017-18 attendance pilot cost NAD 291,000, met jointly by ADEA and the ministry.

Levels in use. Primary and secondary. The 103 schools that piloted attendance capture in School-Link from May 2018 include primary, combined and secondary schools.

How the record is kept. The pilot schools captured each day's teacher and learner attendance, with the reason for absence, and updated School-Link weekly through the trimester ending August 2018, recording 71,387 cases of learner absence. School-Link carries a learner unit record module, which the country calls LURITS. Outside the pilot, the ministry's November 2018 report with ADEA has paper registers marked daily by teachers.

Last twelve months. The attendance pilot ran from May to the end of July 2018.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The ministry's report with ADEA, published in November 2018, says 807 public schools out of 1,848 schools are connected to School-Link, at all levels together. Daily attendance was entered by the 103 pilot schools.

Not held. Nothing held is dated after 2018, so the system's present ownership, plan, budget and direction are not established. The 807 schools are connected, not shown entering data, and no figure separates primary schools.

NER.short: School heads filled printed forms for the yearly school count in 2025; how schools keep pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not held. No dated statement says whether primary schools keep their pupils' records on paper, and nothing held describes a system with a record for each pupil.

NGA.short: A national learner number was launched in 2026 and issued first to examination candidates; whether any primary school enters learners' records is not known.
NGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Federal Ministry of Education launched the Learner Identification Number as its own system, on its statement of 9 April 2026. Biometric Update, on 5 August 2026, names the ministry as the body that, with NIMC, linked the learner numbers to the national identity number registry.

Levels in use. In the first phase the numbers went to candidates registered for the 2026 WAEC and NECO examinations.

How the record is kept. Admission into Edo State's public primary and junior secondary schools is entirely manual, on forms and photocopied certificates, state officials told the News Agency of Nigeria in a report of 31 July 2026. At Nassarawo Primary School in Adamawa State a teacher marks about 50 pupils' attendance each day by hand in a paper register, DPI Africa reported on 12 March 2026.

Last twelve months. The learner number began rolling out in April 2026, with 1.9 million issued. From 14 September 2026 every public and private school in Lagos State must take each learner's residents' registration number at admission and enter it in its records, towards a state database of learners.

Primary schools doing the digital input. Oyo State's system to give every child a learner number was still under development on 31 July 2026. Edo State plans a system tracking each student, and the one it runs takes school-level data, DHIS2 stated on 30 May 2025.

Not held. Which school levels use the learner number, who enters it, and whether any primary school fills the register. The paper statements cover one state's admissions and one school, and no plan or finance for the system is stated.

RWA.short: Primary schools keep a profile per pupil with exam results, and a daily attendance app is live (2026); the share of schools is not known.
RWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. HISP Rwanda, on a page of 7 May 2026, names the Ministry of Education as owner of the KARAME attendance app. The Education Sector Strategic Plan 2024-2029 lists improving digital attendance tracking and an early warning response system among its interventions.

Levels in use. UNICEF Rwanda, on 12 June 2024, describes the School Data Management System, SDMS, in use at Nyarubuye Primary School in Rwamagana District, where the head teacher enters the data.

How the record is kept. SDMS holds a profile for each student and captures national examination results, a World Bank study presented in February 2024 found. In KARAME, teachers and headteachers record each student's daily attendance at the school, and the data syncs to the national education server, on HISP Rwanda's account of May 2026.

Last twelve months. The ministry rolled out a new digital attendance tracking system, The New Times reported on 23 December 2025. HISP Rwanda reported on 11 February 2026 a mission to strengthen the absence tracking system and move its technical support to the local team.

Primary schools doing the digital input. KARAME is live and supports the monitoring of 177,000 reintegrated students, as HISP Rwanda stated in May 2026. The same body names two schools using the absence tracking system, and the World Bank study describes SDMS as in use by schools and teachers.

Not held. A share or count of primary schools entering attendance or results, and whether attendance reaches SDMS per learner or as a monthly total. Nothing is held on rural schools or on current finance.

SDN.short: The ministry counts schools by survey (2026); how primary schools keep their pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not held. Any dated statement of how primary schools keep their learners' records, on paper or otherwise, and any fact on a system holding a record per learner.

SEN.short: A December 2025 brief describes paper-based school data collection; whether primary schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
SEN.summary: Not held. No dated statement says that primary schools keep their pupils' records on paper only, and nothing held describes a system with a record for each pupil, in preparation, on pilot or in use.

SLE.short: In 2022-23 a rollout gave 300 primary schools tablets to enter each pupil's daily attendance; how many do so is not known.
SLE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. What the country calls Wi De Ya is led by the Teaching Service Commission with the Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education and was built by CGA Technologies, as stated in 2024, with funding from the Multi Donor Trust Fund of the World Bank, GPE, the EU, Irish Aid and FCDO. The ministry's Unique Learner ID initiative, reported in April 2026, is funded by GPE and sits within a 2024-2027 programme aligned with the Education Sector Plan 2022-2026.

Levels in use. Wi De Ya was rolled out to primary schools in academic year 2022-23 and was not in use in early childhood centres or secondary schools.

How the record is kept. School leaders enter each learner's profile and daily attendance on the school's tablet, submitting attendance at the end of the school day, and the data appears on dashboards for the commission and the ministry, as reported in 2023.

Last twelve months. The ministry has launched an initiative to build a learner-centred data system, reported in April 2026, whose Unique Learner ID system is to be piloted in four districts, in at least 20 schools in each.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The rollout phase of 2022-23 covered 300 selected primary schools, each given a tablet and training; reporting rates for learner attendance varied by chiefdom and were lower in some rural ones. Rollouts to 1,500 and then 4,000 schools were planned.

Not held. How many of the 300 schools enter data, and the total of primary schools to set them against, are not given. Nothing describes Wi De Ya in use after 2023, or says whether the rollouts to 1,500 and 4,000 schools took place.

SOM.short: A daily per-pupil attendance app was on trial in 42 schools in Puntland State in May 2022; what has happened since is not known.
SOM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In May 2022 the Puntland education ministry proposed to expand what it calls the Digital Attendance Application and took on the collection and analysis of its attendance data, with the roll-out placed under a US$3.35 million GPE programme running May 2022 to April 2023, UNICEF the grant agent.

Levels in use. The application's 2019 pilot in Puntland was in 3 primary schools.

How the record is kept. The application collects daily student and teacher attendance on mobile devices, offline where needed, and uploads it to the server of what Puntland calls its EMIS, as described in May 2022. In 2019 the pilot schools moved from a paper attendance tracker to the application, which records each student's attendance daily with reasons for absence.

Last twelve months. In May 2022 state-wide collection of attendance data was not in place in Puntland and the state's EMIS was under development.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The application was on trial in 42 schools in Puntland State in May 2022, after the 2019 pilot in 3 primary schools.

Not held. Nothing is dated after May 2022, so whether the planned roll-out to about sixty schools took place is not established, and the level of the 42 trial schools is not stated. Nothing held describes a per-pupil record outside Puntland.

SSD.short: Teachers reported each absent pupil by text message in 2024; the share of primary schools doing so is not known.
SSD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The schools' attendance system, which the country calls SSSAMS, was developed under and is supported by the Girls' Education South Sudan programme of the Ministry of General Education and Instruction, funded by UK aid, as its site stated in December 2024. A separate system for refugee learners is managed by UNHCR, on a working paper of September 2025.

Levels in use. The attendance system's tables for academic year 2024 count primary, secondary and other schools in every state. The refugee system reports on early childhood, primary and secondary education, in refugee-hosting schools and camps only.

How the record is kept. The attendance system takes enrolment from the class registers every year; head teachers add and remove pupils by SMS, and class teachers report each absent pupil by SMS to the free number 6464, as of December 2024. An African Union release of March 2026 states that school-level collection relies heavily on handwritten classroom registers and school record books.

Last twelve months. In March 2026 the African Union reported visits to public schools in Juba, where data moved from paper registers to state-level aggregation and national reporting.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The attendance system's panel for academic year 2024 showed 6,650 schools of all levels as having reported attendance at least once, beside 5,915 open schools holding enrolment for the year and 1,321 messages from 3 phones in the last month. An app holding individual pupil records was being piloted in South Sudan in September 2024.

Not held. No share of primary schools reporting attendance is held, nor a count of them given with its total. No current plan for the attendance system is held, and nothing dated in the past twelve months says whether it is advancing or falling back.

STP.short: Schools sent data to the ministry's school-management system in 2023; whether primary schools keep a per-pupil record is not known, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not held. No dated statement says whether primary schools keep their pupils' records on paper, and nothing held describes a system with a record for each pupil that a school adds to during the year.

SWZ.short: A per-pupil record has covered all 976 primary and secondary schools since March 2024; how many primary schools enter attendance or results is not known.
SWZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Education and Training designed and scaled the system, with help from UNICEF and civil society, and its departments presented their uses of it in February 2025. Its EMIS Unit runs regular webinars for users on data entry, validation and extraction, as of November 2025. The ministry is named as a funding partner beside UNICEF Eswatini, GPE KIX and UNESCO Eswatini, on a page of 2024.

Levels in use. The Budget Speech of February 2024 describes a web-based system designed to capture data on individual learners in Grade 0, primary and high schools by their Personal Identification Numbers. In October 2025 it covered primary and secondary schools.

How the record is kept. As of February 2025, information on each learner, such as demographics and performance, is captured with tools that collect it at the school level. The ministry holds learner-level data under unique personal identification numbers, including each learner's orphan status and bursary, as of November 2025.

Last twelve months. In November 2025 the team behind the software called the system fully operational.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The system, launched nationally in March 2024, covers all 976 primary and secondary schools, a figure for schools covered that a GPE KIX blog gave in October 2025. The app that takes attendance, which Eswatini calls SEMIS, was still a pilot with its roll-out to come in October 2025.

Not held. No figure is held for primary schools entering attendance or results during the year, and how often a school adds to a learner's record is not stated. No current plan is held, and nothing dated in the past twelve months says whether the system is advancing or falling back.

SYC.short: The ministry trained school leadership teams on its pupil record platform in 2026; whether any school enters attendance or results is not known.
SYC.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A Ministry of Education team ran the schools' training on what it calls the "MoE Seychelles" OpenEMIS platform, in a post published in March 2026. The attendance guide is issued by the EMIS helpdesk of the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information, on a page published in October 2025.

Levels in use. The training was for the leadership teams of primary and secondary schools across Mahé: headteachers, deputies and office managers.

How the record is kept. The helpdesk gives the procedure for recording attendance in OpenEMIS on the web: under the school, by academic period, week, day, class and grade, each student is present by default and is changed to an excused or unexcused absence.

Last twelve months. The training published in March 2026 covered student admissions, promotions and transfers, classes and subjects, and staff records.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The training published in March 2026 reached school leadership teams across Mahé.

Not held. No report of a school entering attendance or results is held, and nor is which levels use the platform or a count or share of primary schools. No plan or finance for it is held.

TCD.short: Schools filled the yearly school count on paper in 2021; how primary schools keep pupils' records is not known, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not held. Nothing held states how primary schools keep their pupils' records. The one statement on paper, from 2021, is about the yearly census questionnaire.

TGO.short: The ministry launched pupil numbering and designed its platform in 2023; whether any school yet uses it is not known.
TGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The primary and secondary education ministry (MEPS) launched the registration of pupils with a number in 2023. A minister's service note of 2 August 2021 gave the building of a single platform for pupils' marks to the ministry's own centre, CNDP-TICE.

Levels in use. The marks platform ordered in August 2021 was for all public and private schools, consultable at every level of the system.

How the record is kept. The independent panel advising the Global Partnership for Education found on 8 April 2024 no clear evidence that Togo has student identification numbers.

Last twelve months. The joint sector review's aide-mémoire of June 2025 reports the 2023 launch of pupil numbering.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The 2023 work was the design of the enrolment platform that generates the pupils' numbers. The panel said in April 2024 that an automatic data collection system was still being developed.

Not held. No school is named as using the pupil-numbering platform and no pilot is reported; the marks platform was ordered in 2021, not built. No level, plan, finance or event in the last twelve months is held.

TUN.short: In December 2023, 92.7% of public primary schools were on the ministry's school system; how many enter attendance or results is not known.
TUN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The education ministry's digital transformation strategy, presented by its national centre for technologies in education in December 2023, has the development of digital school services as one of its fields. The ministry runs the portal it calls Vie scolaire and publishes the enrolment figures from it.

Levels in use. The centre's December 2023 presentation names Madrassati for the primary stage and EduservPlus for preparatory and secondary.

How the record is kept. The services listed for schools in December 2023 include uploading pupils' absences, sanctions and marks, with the rate of uploading absences given as 2% for the primary stage and 71% for preparatory and secondary. Children entering the first year of basic education in 2025/26 were registered once, by their parents online or by the regional education delegations, and each given a unique identifier.

Last twelve months. Vie scolaire was launched at the end of July 2026, and ministry figures put 53 per cent of all pupils as enrolled on it for 2026/2027 at 20 August 2026. On 7 September 2026 the secondary teachers' federation called on school staff to boycott the ministry's new platform until it works, reporting failures in enrolment and pupil transfers.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The centre counted 4,322 of 4,662 public primary establishments (92.7%) and 52 of 721 private ones on Madrassati in December 2023.

Not held. No share or count of primary schools entering attendance or results is held, nor what the 2% rate for primary absences is a share of. The strategy's period, the source of finance and the school levels using the 2026 platform are not held.

TZA.short: Heads and teachers in one council were trained on a school record system in January 2026; whether any primary school enters attendance is not known.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Prime Minister's Office (TAMISEMI) directed that the School Information System come into official use when schools opened on 13 January 2026, Handeni Town Council's education officer says. The education ministry's Permanent Secretary announced a planned student-tracking system as the ministry's own in November 2025.

Levels in use. Handeni Town Council trained the heads of its primary and secondary schools and one teacher from each school on the system on 9 January 2026.

How the record is kept. A primary head teacher trained in Handeni says a pupil marked absent three times in a row triggers a message to the parent, and the head of Mshikamano Primary School says the school kept its data on paper before the system. An August 2025 investigation in Mbeya District Council describes digital systems designed to track attendance and examination results, which teachers are expected to use daily.

Last twelve months. The Handeni training of 9 January 2026 came ahead of the official start of use directed for 13 January. In November 2025 the government was preparing a system to follow each learner from early childhood to higher education.

Primary schools doing the digital input. In Handeni every head and one teacher per school was trained on 9 January 2026. In Mbeya District Council in August 2025, one school in every five surveyed had a single teacher with a basic understanding of the systems, none formally trained, the Rural Youth Collective reports.

Not held. Nothing shows a primary school entering attendance or results after the start directed for 13 January 2026, and no count of schools trained or using the system is held. No plan or source of finance is held.

UGA.short: In 2025, 58.9% of all primary schools uploaded pupils' enrolment details to the national register; whether any enter attendance or results is not known.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Guidelines of 8 June 2026 make the Ministry of Education and Sports primary custodian of all information entered into the system. An Auditor General's report, reported on 9 June 2026, finds that its administration and configuration remain largely with the vendor, SMSOne, under the ICT ministry's supervision.

Levels in use. For the 2025 academic year 7,408 pre-primary, 26,597 primary and 4,571 secondary schools responded, the ministry reports.

How the record is kept. The system collects data on each learner, issues a Learner Identification Number and tracks transfers, with 11,787,396 primary learners registered at December 2025. School heads register the learners.

Last twelve months. In January 2026 the ministry published its first annual statistical abstract since 2017, compiled from the system for the 2025 academic year. It launched the new guidelines on 8 June 2026, with sanctions for institutions that fail their data obligations, and the contractor was reported on 9 June 2026 to be upgrading the platform to a second version.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The ministry reports that 26,597 of the country's 45,164 primary schools (58.9%) responded to the data upload for 2025: 12,511 of 12,544 government schools and 14,086 of 32,620 private schools.

Not held. No source describes schools entering attendance or results: what is held is the registration of learners, transfers and a yearly upload. No plan, source of finance or share for rural schools is held.

ZAF.short: Schools record attendance and marks digitally and a national register holds each pupil, in 2025; the share of primary schools doing so is not known.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Department of Basic Education's 2025/26 Annual Performance Plan says SA-SAMS, the school administration system, is developed and maintained by the Department. The plan commits the Department to modernise it into a web-enabled platform with the National Education Collaboration Trust and lists that modernisation among unfunded mandates.

Levels in use. The Minister of Basic Education's written reply says LURITS, the Department's learner register, holds data for each learner and tracked learners in Grades 1 to 11 across its 2020 to 2025 datasets. The plan's aim is that all public schools use SA-SAMS, with no level named.

How the record is kept. A study published in November 2024 found eight rural schools in iLembe district using SA-SAMS to manage attendance and track performance, with admin clerks entering the data at the school. The 2025/26 plan says schools are to upload General Education Certificate scores onto SA-SAMS, and term 4 schedules are extracted from it.

Last twelve months. The Minister's reply gives learner totals from LURITS for 2020 to 2025, the 2025 dataset preliminary.

Primary schools doing the digital input. The Department says about 99.9% of functional ordinary schools of all levels (24,850 schools in 2024) had their databases uploaded to LURITS and the provincial data warehouses as of July 2024, which is a share of schools whose database was uploaded. The plan measures the percentage of public schools reporting through SA-SAMS and says the Western Cape does not collect source data through it.

Not held. No share or count of primary schools entering attendance or results during the year is held; the one share held counts schools of all levels whose database was uploaded. Nothing dated in the last twelve months is held, and no budget line for the system.

ZMB.short: Schools report enrolment yearly on paper, by a 2025 account; how they keep pupil records is not known, so no stage is set.
ZMB.summary: Not held. No dated statement of how primary schools keep their learners' records is held. No system holding a record for each learner that a primary school adds to during the year is described.

ZWE.short: The ministry said in 2026 its system tracks each pupil's absence and grades; how many primary schools enter them is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education presents the system it calls EMIS, and the report drawn from it, as its own, with its spokesperson speaking for it in June 2026.

Levels in use. The ministry's EMIS report counts 39,736 learners who dropped out in 2025, 13,032 at primary and 26,704 at secondary level, and the ministry describes its Early Warning System without limiting it to either level.

How the record is kept. The ministry's spokesperson said in June 2026 that the Early Warning System, now integrated into EMIS, flags individual learners by tracking persistent absenteeism and falling grades and produces a real-time list of learners absent for extended periods.

Last twelve months. The spokesperson said in June 2026 that the Early Warning System is being rolled out with re-entry and community tracing, and that the government will keep strengthening it.

Primary schools doing the digital input. School-based response teams act on the system's flags, and district and school authorities use its list of absent learners, the ministry said in June 2026.

Not held. Who enters the attendance and grades, and where, is not held, nor any count or share of schools in the Early Warning System. No plan or source of finance for it is held.
